News.title: Zelensky’s ‘WW3’ masterstroke? How drawing Iran into Ukraine war could spell doom for Putin’s invasion…with Trump’s help
News.content:
UKRAINE has given Vladimir Putin a major headache by dragging Iran towards the Ukraine war and giving Donald Trump a reason to tighten the screws on Moscow.

Kyiv’s daring drone strike on an Iranian military cargo ship in the Caspian Sea sparked threats from Tehran that may see two conflicts collide.



As opposing allies become drawn into the conflict, experts say Volodymyr Zelensky could seal a World War Three-style showdown to defeat Putin.

Ukraine’s attack on Iran targeted a supply line that the Kremlin has used to import lethal Shahed suicide drones and missiles from the pariah state since 2022.



It marked the first direct clash between the two nations since Russia‘s invasion.

Iran claimed that the vessel was purely commercial and vowed to respond – declaring that the “hostile and criminal” strike “cannot go unanswered”.

But the move could position Ukraine as an ally to Trump in a shadow war against the anti-Western axis.

Foreign policy experts say it could be a high-risk strategy from Zelensky to convince the US president to tighten the screws on Putin.



Dr Richard Arnold, an Eastern European security expert, told The Sun: “Ukraine wants to be in Trump’s good books.

“Trump has shown a lot of frustration with Nato allies who have not come to his aid and it appears Zelensky’s almost trying to say, ‘look, we’re the better partner than your Nato partners.'”

Dr Arnold suggested that Ukraine may be positioning itself as an anti-Iran shield.

Zelensky is “trying to build up the image of Ukraine as the Israel of Eastern Europe,” he said.

Since the outbreak of the Iran war, Kyiv has provided the US with technical expertise to counter the Iranian Shahed drones – weapons that Russia has used extensively to attack Ukrainian cities.



Professor Mikhail Alexseev, a political science expert at San Diego University, said it is a calculated move to drum up support in Washington.

He told The Sun: “For Ukraine, it’s very important to have the United States on its side. Ukraine needs to show Trump that it has the cards.

“This is one of the cards – that it can help the United States prevail in achieving objectives in Iran, with having its nuclear program suppressed and ensuring security in the Strait of Hormuz.”



After attacking the Iranian ship, Zelensky revealed that Russia has been feeding Tehran satellite intelligence to strike American military bases in the Gulf.

He said: “There is a clear correlation between Russia’s satellite imagery of these sites and Iranian strikes – both before the attacks, in preparation for them, and afterward, to assess the damage inflicted.”

The Ukrainian leader promised to share the intel with Washington – but made a point of aligning the US and Ukraine’s ambitions.

He said: “None of us in the world should turn a blind eye to one very simple fact: evil always seeks ways to make things worse and spread further.

“Russia must be stopped. This war must be stopped. Pressure on the aggressor must work.”



Zelensky’s bid to win over the White House appears to have been paying dividends.

At the Nato summit in Ankara, Trump said he would grant Ukraine the game-changing licence to build state-of-the-art Patriot missile interceptors.

It may prove decisive in dismantling Putin’s last major advantage – Russia’s missile capabilities – with Zelensky claiming the “battle in the sky” will be key to winning the war.



Ukraine has been desperate to bolster its rapidly-depleting stockpile of interceptors amid a slew of deadly ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv.

But the growing alignment between Washington and Kyiv could prompt Putin to pile more support behind Iran and deepen the conflict.

Arnold said: “It gives Russia a powerful incentive not to let Iran fail. That’s how this war becomes almost unstoppable.”

He warned that “escalation of the conflict is far more likely than resolution”.

It comes after Nato scrambled fighter jets after a Russian Kh-101 missile smashed into Poland this week.



Washington previously warned that Putin could be plotting an armed attack on Poland to test the international alliance – as it faces calls to fight back.

Alexseev said that the conflict has been moving in the direction of an all-out global war for some time.

He explained: “Russia’s war against Ukraine has been not just a small regional war, but a much broader international conflict from the get-go.



“We have seen the way that Russia aligned its forces, counting on economic support from India and China, on military support with Shahed drones and ballistic missile technology from Iran, with troops and artillery ammunition from North Korea.

“Wars, particularly involving great powers, rarely can be contained on a regional scale.”

As the Ukraine and the Iran wars collide, experts fear allies on both sides could be dragged into World War Three.

Alekseev said: “We’re moving into the kind of environment where conflict is normalised, everybody retaliates, nobody takes a step back, and we’re approaching the kind of conditions that led to larger wars in the past.”

Arnold warned: “There are a lot of voices, unfortunately, saying we are in what is called the pre-war period.



“Scholars have been noting for some time how similar the world of today looks to the world before World War One.”

Meanwhile, the strain on Putin’s weakening war machine has backed the dictator into a corner.

Kremlin Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said the country is enduring a “very difficult period”, and Putin recently made the rare admission that the country is “struggling” with an energy crisis.



Dwindling manpower has seen Moscow deploy 30,000 North Korean troops and parliament allow even the most hardened criminals to be drafted.

Arnold said: “Russia is facing a manpower problem, simply because it hasn’t got enough people to power its industries and fight the war in Ukraine.”

Russia has suffered 1.4 million casualties since invading Ukraine in 2022, including an estimated 500,000 deaths.

A report last month showed that the average life expectancy for Russian troops on the frontline was just 20 minutes.

Zelensky warned that Putin may declare another full-scale mobilisation after September’s elections and Moscow struggles to sustain the war effort.



The move may be a response to the recent endgame blitz that Ukraine has targeted at key Russian infrastructure over the summer.

Zelensky said Putin will only end the fighting once he is beaten.

The Ukrainian president told Sky News: “What we tried to do to make this challenge also for Russians; otherwise, they will not feel that the war is everywhere…

“That’s why we started to do everything to respond and to bring this war back to Russia, where it came to us… and that’s why we started our mid-strikes and deep-strike operations, just to respond.”

Alexseev stressed that while cracks are appearing on the Russian front, Ukraine’s Western allies must do far more to force Putin to backtrack.

He said: “Putin is very stubborn and Russia is a big, resourceful, rich country. The pressure signals moves in the right direction, but it’s not yet enough.

“A lot more has to be done, both in terms of supporting Ukraine with greater capabilities and in terms of repositioning globally against Russia.”

News.title: I spent years finding long-lost mum & made shock discovery that cracked 50-year cold case… truth was right under my nose
News.content:
DESPERATE for answers about his biological mother, Richard Hanchett had no idea his quest would solve one of the greatest murder mysteries that had baffled cops for nearly 50 years.

During efforts to find the woman who gave him up for adoption, Richard, unravelled the shocking truth that his mum had been right under his nose the whole time.



It turned out she was at the centre of the decades-long cold case.

“I had no idea in the world where it was going to go or anything,” Richard Hanchett told Oxygen.com.



In 1974, an auburn haired woman’s mutilated woman was discovered abandoned in the windswept dunes of Cape Cod.

Lying on a beach towel was the naked body of the woman whose skull had been savagely crushed.



Her hands had been severed in what investigators believed was a calculated attempt to prevent identification through fingerprints.

A young girl was out walking the family dog with her parents when she stumbled upon the woman’s lifeless body sprawled among the sand dunes.

Her pale, motionless form lay exposed on the beach, her pink-painted toenails still eerily neat against the sand. Beside her head sat a pair of jeans and a blue bandana.

Despite years of detective work, forensic examinations and countless public appeals, the victim’s identity remained maddeningly elusive.



The case was dubbed “The Lady of the Dunes” in every newspaper in the city that Richard, from the Detroit suburbs, had walked past and gazed at – never knowing that the woman was his biological mother.

The mystery snowballed into one of America’s defining cold cases, generating a maze of theories and suspected links to notorious killers.

But nothing was ever linked back to the nameless woman whose story remained a mystery for nearly five decades.



The mystery body was exhumed on three occasions, 1980, 2000 and 2013.

Clay composites were made of her head – hoping someone in the world might recognise her.

Then, a potential breakthrough came from an unlikely source – Joe Hill, the son of literary giant Stephen King.

He had followed the case closely and become fascinated by the mystery surrounding the woman’s identity.

In 2015, Joe was watching a 40th anniversary screening of Jaws, filmed in Massachusetts during the summer of 1974 – around the same time the Lady of the Dunes was believed to have been in Provincetown, roughly 100 miles from the production.



Just over halfway through the film, something on the screen stopped him cold.

Among the crowds was a young woman who looked remarkably like the composite image of the unidentified victim Joe knew so well.

She appeared to be around 30, with her hair pulled back in a bandanna and blue jeans on – details that immediately caught his attention.

Joe wondered whether he had stumbled across the woman’s last known sighting, captured entirely by chance on film.

Jaws screenwriter Carl Gottlieb later heard about Hill’s discovery and dug out the production records.



The timing appeared to fit, with the woman visible in Scene 130, around 54 minutes into the film, as crowds boarded a ferry.

There was, however, no record of her being a hired extra for the scene.

She may simply have been a tourist caught in the background as she boarded the ferry.

Still, the footage offered investigators an extraordinary possibility – that the woman on screen was the Lady of the Dunes, travelling towards Cape Cod in the final days before she was killed.

In 2018, Richard’s submitted his DNA to Ancestry.com and matched with his living cousin, revealing the name of his mother to be Ruth Marie Terry.



But neither Richard nor the cops knew that Ruth was dead, or, crucially, that she was “The Lady of the Dunes”.

Years on, as technology advanced, investigators used the bone samples collected after exhumation used them for DNA testing in 2022.

Her profile immediately flagged genetic ties to living relatives in Tennessee and Michigan – where her son Richard Hanchett’s DNA was registered.



Genealogists used these distant and close cousin matches to build out her family tree, confirming her identity as 37-year-old Ruth Marie Terry within a few months.

Weeks before the FBI called Richard to confirm the Lady of the Dunes was in fact his real mum, he recalled having dreams about her murder.

“I was having nightmares for about three weeks… and I didn’t know what it meant; I couldn’t figure it out,” Hanchett claimed.

After hearing from the cops, he said the meaning behind his dreams became “very apparent.”

He even described to agents that he kept “seeing this guy hit a woman in the back of the head and crush her skull,” details that piqued the agency’s curiosity.



The discovery transformed Richard from an ordinary adoptee searching for his roots into the son of one of America’s most recognisable unidentified murder victims.

Back in 1958, Ruth had given birth to a son while living in Michigan.

Unable to raise the baby herself, she arranged for him to be adopted by her workplace superintendent, Richard Hanchett Sr., and his wife.

Richard said he had “such a happy life” with the couple that adopted him but could not shake off his curiosity about his real mum.

Once Ruth’s identity had finally been restored, detectives rapidly reconstructed the final chapter of her life.



Their investigation led them to her husband, Guy Rockwell Muldavin, an antiques dealer and convicted fraudster who also used several aliases, including Raoul Guy Rockwell.

The couple had married only months before Ruth vanished in 1974.

Cape and Islands District Attorney Robert Galibois announced investigators had concluded that Muldavin was responsible for Ruth’s murder.



Because Muldavin died in 2002, he will never face trial.

Family members recalled that Muldavin exhibited possessive behavior around Ruth.

When Muldavin returned alone after their summer 1974 trip driving her car, he told her family that he and Ruth had gotten into a fight during their travel and that she had gone missing.

He also told other witnesses that she had died.

Her family never saw or heard from her again.



Police also established that he disposed of her possessions, emptied her accounts and liquidated her belongings shortly after her disappearance.

The findings echoed disturbing events from years earlier.

In 1960, Muldavin had been the prime suspect in the disappearance of his second wife, Manzanita Rockwell, and his teenage stepdaughter, Dolores Mearns, in Seattle.

Human remains were later discovered in a septic tank at his property, although he was never convicted over those deaths.

Investigators have said Muldavin repeatedly preyed upon women, exploiting relationships for financial gain before disappearing from their lives.



With Ruth’s identification and the conclusions of the investigation, one of Massachusetts’ oldest unidentified homicide victims has finally reclaimed her name.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

For Richard, the search that began with a longing to know his mother ended by exposing the devastating truth behind one of America’s darkest unsolved killings.

The mystery that haunted generations has at last been given an answer.

News.title: Top cop accused of having sex with two junior colleagues was paid £55k after he quit the force
News.content:
SEX PROBE Top cop accused of having sex with two junior colleagues was paid £55k after he quit the force

A FORMER chief constable accused of having sex while on duty was paid more than £55,000 after quitting the force, it has been revealed.

Scott Chilton resigned with immediate effect following 33 years of service after the police watchdog announced he was under investigation for gross misconduct over alleged sexual relationships with two junior colleagues.



Now, figures have revealed that Mr Chilton received £55,154 as “compensation for loss of employment” following his sudden departure from Hampshire Police.

The sum is understood to relate to a payment in lieu of working his three-month contractual notice period.



The former top cop is accused of having a sexual relationship with a more junior officer while serving as chief constable.

He is further alleged to have had sex with another junior officer while on duty earlier in his policing career.

Details of the allegations emerged after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) launched a gross misconduct investigation into his behaviour.

The misconduct notice alleges that Mr Chilton abused “his position for a sexual purpose having a sexual relationship with an officer while chief constable and failed to declare this relationship”.

He is also accused of failing to “disclose a previous sexual relationship with another officer during the application process to become chief constable”.

Investigators allege that he “repeatedly and dishonestly” denied the allegations when questioned by senior figures in the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner.



Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones met Mr Chilton at her home in November 2024 to discuss his future.

The pair met again at police headquarters on February 12, 2025, before Ms Jones made a formal referral to the IOPC on February 26, 2025.

Mr Chilton is due to face a formal misconduct hearing in October, where the allegations against him will be formally considered.

Explaining why the former officer received the substantial sum after resigning, a police spokesperson confirmed the payment details.

“On Mr Chilton’s resignation, he received £55,154 as Pay in Lieu of Notice (as opposed to him working the three month period in his contract),” the spokesperson said.



A former detective, Mr Chilton spent around 33 years in policing after joining the service at the age of 18.

He landed the top job in Hampshire in February 2023, transferring back to the force after serving as chief constable in Dorset from August 2021.

Following his sudden resignation, Alexis Boon has replaced Mr Chilton as Chief Constable of Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) are investigating the claims.

Director Derrick Campbell, previously said: “Any allegations involving officers abusing their position for a sexual purpose are taken extremely seriously.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“At the end of our investigation, we found evidence to indicate that the former chief constable’s conduct may have breached the police standards of professional behaviour.

“We have decided that Mr Chilton should face a disciplinary hearing. It will now be for the PCC to arrange these proceedings in due course, where a disciplinary panel will then determine, based on the evidence, whether the gross misconduct allegations are proven.”

News.title: Inside the sick minds of false rape accusers making life-changing allegations for money & sympathy as Brit, 26, jailed
News.content:
CASH, attention, undue sympathy – what drives someone to falsely accuse another person of rape?

As a young British woman is jailed in Hong Kong for blackmailing a banker with a false rape claim, the chilling psychology behind such a torturous and life-altering crime is more complex than it might first appear.



Isabel Rose, 26, from Hackney, East London, was last week sentenced to six years behind bars for blackmail and perverting the course of justice.

She demanded £100,000 from an anonymous banker, threatening to report him to the police.



But there are many hidden motives behind this rare but twisted crime beyond the allure of cold hard cash, experts told The Sun – as the judge who sentenced “wicked” Rose appeared to hint at.

Judge Adriana Noelle Tse Ching slammed Rose, saying she had “not shown an iota of remorse for her wicked behaviour”.

The judge said she had taken advantage of the man she accused’s “kindness, naivety, friendship and romantic interest”.

Dr André De Zutter, a legal psychologist and a leading expert on fake rape claims, said victims of false complaints “say it’s the worst thing that can happen to you, because even your own mother is disgusted by you”.

Rather than being meticulously planned, fake rape allegations are normally opportunistic – accusers use them to get out of a corner or, in rare cases, to make a frantic grab for cash.

Dr De Zutter said: “It’s an impulsive act out of desperation. You’re in a corner, you don’t know what to do. And that seems the only way out.”



People who fabricate rape rarely “have a good life” he said, adding that making a fake rape claim, “for a lot of women, is an unthinkable crime“.

But in Rose’s case, the allure of callous financial gain was irresistible regardless of the agony it would cause – and appeared to be more thought-out than most false rape claims.

Rose had met the banker while travelling in Thailand in January 2024. A month later she flew to meet up with him in Hong Kong.

And in devastating series of texts revealed in court, she would go on to torturously try to extract as much cash from her target as possible.

The pair spent the night of February 1 together, but the next morning, Rose sent him a WhatsApp message saying: “Are you annoyed I didn’t want to have sex.”



He replied: “What no of course not. Was impressed by your restraint.”

Later that day, Rose wrote: “You violated me last night, I didn’t wanna have sex.”

Desperate and confused, her victim replied: “I’m really deeply sorry, I was slightly drunk and I misread your signals, it’s no excuse and I know it doesn’t make it any better.”



Later on, Rose delivered the devastating blow – she messaged him claiming: “You basically raped me.”

Days after the alleged assault, Rose demanded £5,000. The man had agreed to reimburse her for her travel and accommodation in Hong Kong, the court heard.

When he sent the cash, she began to ask for “escalating amounts of money” eventually demanding £100,000.

In one message, Rose wrote: “Send me the right amount you owe me for everything. Think about that. Think carefully.”

She added: “You’ve given 10% of what I’m owed. 100% of my soul gone.”



Her victim pleaded: “But I don’t have 100k, I have no way of paying you that.”

Rose then filed a police report claiming the man had raped her.

He was arrested, but released within hours, and investigators turned their attention to Rose, charging her with blackmail and perverting the course of justice.

The 26-year-old was handed a guilty verdict in March after a six-day trial.

The judge described the banker as an “honest, credible and reliable witness”, whilst Rose was labelled “dishonest, uncredible and unreliable”.



De Zutter said Rose’s case was rare because “mostly, false allegations are about sympathy and attention”.

His studies focus on women who have made fake accusations of rape, because false accusations represent such a tiny slice of all cases, and women are more likely to be raped than men.

He explained that some people make false allegations for attention – both positive and negative.



De Zutter said: “Sympathy is positive attention. But some people also thrive on negative attention.

“If somebody dislikes you, but he calls you every day to say that he dislikes you, that’s also a sort of attention.”

Rape is incredibly difficult to prove, with very few police reports leading to a conviction. Dire chances of justice make it difficult for genuine victims to come forward, with hours of police interviews going over and over a traumatic event hellish for survivors.

But De Zutter said fakers who crave any sort of attention enjoy the process “because they get the attention they normally don’t get”.

He said: “The police talk to them for hours and hours and they are called back again and they are investigated.



“And the person who is making false claims does not mind. There is some gain.”

Stacey Sharples, 31, may be Britain’s most notorious filer of fake rape claims.

She repeatedly sought out men online, making it clear she wanted sex.

Afterwards – sometimes without any sexual activity taking place – she would call the cops and allege she had been raped.

In February, Sharples pleaded guilty to ten counts of perverting the course of justice for filing false rape reports against ten separate men.



Most of the men were arrested or spent time in custody before police untangled her twisted web of lies.

She was handed a four-and-a-half year prison sentence for the fake claims she made.

De Zutter said those who make fake rape accusations often target several people as they become increasingly desperate for attention.

Scrutiny from police or hatred from those they are accusing doesn’t put them off, the psychologist said.

Dr Elizabeth Loftus, a psychologist specialising in false memory, told The Sun that some fake accusers can even believe that a rape happened even if it did not.



She said: “When I get involved in a court case where it appears as if a false accusation is being made, I usually ask the attorney: ‘Do you think she honestly believes it happened or that she is deliberately lying?’

“Both are possibilities. People can come to believe that something happened that did not, especially when they are exposed to a lot of suggestion.”

She added: “People who come to believe that their false memory is authentic have also sought economic ‘compensation’ for what they believe is a harm done to them.”



Dr Felicity Goodyear-Smith told The Sun that fake accusations could come from “misunderstanding, misinterpretation of an event, mistaken identity, contaminated or distorted memory”.

She said they could also follow “unrequited romantic interest” or be to “avoid judgement from others following consensual sex subsequently regretted”.

After attention and financial gain, there is another factor that can lead people to falsely report a rape: to create an alibi, or explain themselves out of a hole, De Zutter said.

He explained: “There are a lot of famous cases where somebody is late and had consensual sex with her boyfriend, but the parents were very strict.

“She comes home and the father is really angry because she is late.



“And then she thinks, ‘If I say that I’m raped, then all this anger turns into sympathy’.”

He said another reason for filing a false rape accusation is when someone has cheated on a partner.

Dr Goodyear-Smith said a made up rape allegation could be used as an alibi to “explain unfaithfulness or unexpected pregnancy” or “account for an unexplained absence”.



Fake rape accusations are devastating for their victims, CEO of the False Allegations Support Organisation Margaret Gardener told The Sun.

She said she had supported “mainly men” and “some women over a 22 years period, accused of both sex offences, including many rapes, and the falsely accused of child protection issues”.

Gardener claimed “those making allegations are supported all the way to the court case”, whereas the accused get “absolutely no support, except for a small number of volunteer falsely accused support groups”.

Dad-of-three Astron Inman said he “felt like a pariah” after Sharples falsely accused him of rape.

He said: “My life was turned upside down. My relationship broke down, I couldn’t see my children. I was panic-stricken.”



“I couldn’t trust anyone. I had a DBS done for a new job and it came back with ‘arrested for rape’ on it. I was mortified. I had a long spell out of work and had to sell my car to make ends meet.

Astron said he will never get back the man he once was.

He said: “I’m glad it’s all over now, but I can’t just put it all behind me. She can pick up the pieces of her life when she’s released, but I can’t. My life has imploded.”

False rape claims remain incredibly rare – but many survivors of sexual violence still struggle to report genuine crimes.

De Zutter said balancing the possibility of a fake accusation is very difficult for investigators.



A man is roughly 230 times more likely to be raped or sexually assaulted than to be the subject of a proven false accusation, analysis by Channel 4 showed.

De Zutter explained: “You cannot go around and say, oh we should be more sceptical of women. Because then you would not trust a lot of women who are actually raped or sexually assaulted.

“If you would trust all victims, we would make a mistake 1 in 20 times.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“But if you distrust all victims, we make a mistake 19 out of 20 times.

“So it’s always better to be trustworthy, empathetic, sympathetic – but that’s the area where a false complainant manoeuvre.”

News.title: Woman, 33, ‘drugged & kept as sex slave’ found handcuffed to balcony by horrified neighbours as 2 teens among 4 arrested
News.content:
DEPRAVED ABUSE Woman, 33, ‘drugged & kept as sex slave’ found handcuffed to balcony by horrified neighbours as 2 teens among 4 arrested

A HOMELESS woman allegedly drugged and kept as a sex slave for months was found handcuffed on a balcony by a horrified neighbour.

A local initially believed the half-naked woman was a leftover Halloween decoration before phoning cops with four men, including two teenagers, being charged over the alleged campaign of abuse.



German investigators say the neighbour likely saved the woman’s life as she was found suffering from severe hypothermia with bruises and wounds over her body.

She had allegedly been held captive from July to November 2025.



Cops say the men lured the 33-year-old into their home in Soest with food and shelter before executing a merciless campaign of torture and rape.

Investigators told local paper SauerlandKurier: “The woman was kept like a slave in the cellar.



“Everything imaginable was done to her – and much more, even resulting in permanent disfigurement.”

The woman spent several months in hospital.

Remarkably, local residents did not hear her screaming – even when she was hanging from the balcony for several hours.

Miriam Becker told German press WDR: “I was very shocked that we as neighbors didn’t notice what was going on.”



Another claimed: “She was definitely drugged.”

The suspected abusers reportedly filmed themselves beating the alleged victim.

The partner of the alleged ringleader was also living in the house with her two children, but has not been charged, reported SauerlandKurier.



Investigators told the paper that the alleged victim may have been suffering from Stockholm syndrome and had formed a bond with her suspected abusers.

She reportedly feared she would not survive the winter without staying in the house.

Now four men have been charged with aggravated assault, trafficking in cannabis, and rape.

Two of the alleged rapists are still minors at just 16 and 17 years old.

The other two suspects are aged 24 and 29, with the older one considered to be the group’s ringleader.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

All four hold German passports, and the 29-year-old was already known to police.

The trial begins in October and will include 12 hearings, according to a spokesperson for Arnsberg Regional Court.

News.title: Greek ‘FBI’ joins suitcase death probe as cops reveal no fingerprints or DNA found after Brit woman found dead
News.content:
GREECE’S ‘FBI’ has joined the probe into the death of a Brit who was found stuffed in a suitcase in Athens, sparking a major probe.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was discovered by a homeless man in a derelict building in the Kypseli district of the Greek capital on July 18.



An investigation is now underway involving Greek and Brit cops.

Interpol were even involved to help identify the Scotswoman’s body when DNA and fingerprints were found.



Elisabeth’s cause of death has yet to be determined, but homicide cops from Greece‘s national force, the Hellenic Police, are leading the efforts to find answers.

But they have called in backup from the organised crime division – the country’s equivalent to the American FBI.

The unit was set up two years ago to help tackle the country’s most major investigations.

The investigation into Elisabeth’s death is yet to be declared a murder probe – but cops have fast-tracked her autopsy toxicology reports.



Police spokeswoman Konstantina Dimoglidou told the Times: “We have made it a priority so we can have results in the coming days.

“Then we will know how she died. This can’t wait.”

A fresh twist in the probe came when it emerged cops had found no DNA or fingerprints on the suitcase Elisabeth’s body was inside.

It was hoped forensics on the bag would lead to vital clues but nothing was discovered.

It is believed Elisabeth told friends in Greece she was visiting American friends in Kypseli on July 15 but the Americans have yet to be found.



Ms Dimoglidou added: “We’ve had the entire homicide division of the Greek FBI working night and day on the case.

“We’re in contact with other police forces. We’re going to solve this. July 15 was the last day she had contact with any of her friends.

“Our investigations are focused on the intervening days and whom she may have met and where she stayed.



“The Americans have not been identified or found. There is always the possibility that she died and then for some reason was hidden.

“Our priority is to get to the bottom of who left the suitcase. Whoever they were was careful not to leave any fingerprints or DNA.”

It is feared Elisabeth may have been murdered by a homeless man she was helping.

She had carried out charity work across the world.

Local media has reported Elisabeth was seen speaking with homeless people in the area, while Greek cops are said to be looking for a man named “Markos”.



Scottish cops are also believed to be carrying out investigations in Inverness.

It comes as Elisabeth’s heartbroken dad revealed he received haunting text messages from his daughter’s phone after her mysterious death which read: “I need some quiet time, I want to be alone.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Greek officials learned that from July 15 to 29, several messages had been sent to Elisabeth’s relatives pretending to be her.



Elisabeth’s phone was only turned off on Wednesday morning after reports of the body being found made global headlines, local media claim.

News.title: ‘Dangerous’ Brit fugitive, 27, set to go on UK’s Most Wanted list arrested near Spain’s Costa Blanca in major operation
News.content:
FUGITIVE SNARED ‘Dangerous’ Brit fugitive, 27, set to go on UK’s Most Wanted list arrested near Spain’s Costa Blanca in major operation

A “DANGEROUS” British fugitive who was set to go on the UK’s Most Wanted list has been arrested near Spain’s Costa Blanca.

The 27-year-old, accused of firearms offences and drug trafficking, now faces a possible life sentence according to Spanish police.



British authorities issued an international arrest warrant for the suspected criminal in June.

A unit specialising in tracking down on-the-run criminals immediately launched an operation to identify his whereabouts.



After several days the team traced the man to a hide-out in Algorfa, near Alicante.

Spain’s National Police said: “A search and arrest operation was then carried out, allowing officers to intercept and immediately arrest him.”



The force released footage of armed officers confronting and cuffing the shirtless suspect near his home.

Later, footage shows cops escorting the man dressed in a blue t-shirt and shorts into custody.

Cops said the “extremely dangerous” fugitive was set to be added to the UK’s Most Wanted list before his arrest.

He is accused of belonging to an organised crime gang involved in the distribution of cocaine, cannabis and heroin between 2023 and 2024.



And police said the man continued committing crimes while on bail.

“He is accused of serious offences involving the use of firearms against people and posed a high flight risk due to the possibility of a life sentence”, Spanish National Police said.

The suspect has now been brought before Spain’s Central Court, which will begin extradition proceedings to return him to the UK.



He is expected to stand trial in the UK.

It comes after another British man wanted over a horror Costa del Sol shooting was arrested in Colombia after he feld across the Atlantic.

Fugitive Polemos Michael George was seized on an international arrest warrant at Jose Maria Cordova Airport, near the Colombian city of Medellin.

Cops confirmed the Brit was wanted by Spain for attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms after a terrifying gun attack in Marbella.

Footage released by Colombian police shows George being marched away by armed officers before being fingerprinted and forced to pose for a mugshot.



The arrest was confirmed by William Rincon, the newly-appointed director of Colombia’s National Police, who posted the dramatic footage online.

He said: “This outcome is the result of specialist analysis by the National Police and the timely exchange of information with Spanish and UK authorities, which enabled the identification of this man’s presence in the country and the effective execution of his capture.”

Mr Rincon also issued a chilling warning to criminals on the run, declaring: “Crime has no refuge: justice reaches everywhere.”

News.title: Teenage girl, 17, dies at major UK festival headlined by Scissor Sisters and Wolf Alice
News.content:
FESTIVAL TRAGEDY Teenage girl, 17, dies at major UK festival headlined by Scissor Sisters and Wolf Alice

A 17-YEAR-OLD girl has died following a “medical episode” at a major UK festival headlined by the Scissor Sisters and Wolf Alice.

The teenager passed away in the early hours of the morning after suffering the health issue at around 2.15am at Kendal Calling festival in Cumbria.



The popular four-day music and arts festival is held annually at Lowther Deer Park in the Lake District.

Officers have asked for anyone in the Calling Out tent area and the Big Wheel at the time of the episode to get in contact.



Cops and emergency services from the North West Ambulance Service attended and administered CPR.

Cumbria Police said they are looking into the circumstances after the teen was pronounced dead at the scene despite the best efforts of paramedics.



The girl’s family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers, confirmed cops.

Cumbria Police added in a statement: “Our thoughts are with them at this difficult time.

“Officers are particularly keen to speak with a group of women who alerted first responders to the girl after becoming concerned for her welfare.”

A Kendal Calling spokesperson said the festival team was supporting authorities with their investigation.



A statement read: “The team at Kendal Calling are deeply saddened by the passing of a festival attendee in the early hours of Sunday morning following a medical episode.

“As soon as the individual became unwell, they were immediately attended to by our on-site security and medical teams.

“Paramedics and medical personnel provided emergency care at the scene and did everything they could to help.

“We extend our deepest sympathies to the individual’s family, friends and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time.

“We are supporting the relevant authorities and will continue to assist them with their investigation.”



More than 40,000 people have descended on Lowther Deer Park, near Penrith, to camp and watch a variety of acts for the four-day festival.

This year’s high-profile headliners include Wolf Alice, Primal Scream, Biffy Clyro, Scissor Sisters and Groove Armada.

There are a number of other stages and tents featuring DJs, comedy and even a cinema at the festival.

It is also family-friendly with an area called Kids Calling specifically for children.

News.title: Pilot issues 'flying saucer' alert after spotting UFO while landing at Gatwick
News.content:
Pilot issues 'flying saucer' alert after spotting UFO while landing at Gatwick

The pilot of a commercial plane coming in to land at Gatwick Airport reported seeing a "flying saucer" which was terrifyingly just feet away from the aircraft

View Image A pilot told of seeing a "flying saucer" coming in to land at Gatwick Airport (Image: Getty Images)

A pilot of a passenger plane reported a “flying saucer” flying feet away from the aircraft as it came in to land.

‌



The sighting of the suspected drone was highlighted in a report into the incident in April that took place as the plane was preparing to touch down at Gatwick Airport.

‌



The report was among disturbing close encounters of objects with commercial aircraft in the UK, amid high profile disturbances made at airports in recent years caused by drones.

‌



Crew of another plane told investigators a drone had come so close they could make out markings and see its propellers.

In the incident involving the plane coming into Gatwick Airport, investigators at the UK Airprox Board stated: “The A319 pilot reports that descending, turning left, a disc or ‘flying saucer’ type ­suspected drone was seen flying very close in the opposite direction, at the same level to them, past their right wing.

“Approximately 100-300ft from their aircraft wing. The object looked like a disc with darker markings on the rim, a suspected possible drone but not sure. It was very close to the aircraft, but no ­evasive action was required as they were in a turn already.”

‌



Following an assessment of the near-miss, the board concluded that the safety of the jet had been "reduced", according to The Sun.

In a separate incident occurring in the same month near Heathrow Airport involved an A321 aircraft whose crew spotted a drone passing dangerously close.

Official documents state: "The A321 pilot reports that, whilst in a left turn on to base leg at LHR (over Marlow), a drone was witnessed to fly down the left-hand-side of the aircraft at close enough proximity to see details such as the colour, shape and individual props spinning."

Article continues below

Investigating the close call, Airprox officials said: "The board considered that providence had played a major part in the incident and/or a definite risk of collision had existed."

The reports follow another striking encounter detailed by the board involving military personnel. Two Royal Air Force pilots operating an air-to-air refuelling mission at 16,000ft over the North Sea off the Norfolk coast spotted an unidentified craft, reported the Daily Star.

One pilot inside a Voyager tanker was forced to duck as the object zoomed past at a distance of just 100ft to 150ft. Although the pilot of an accompanying Typhoon fighter also witnessed the object, it failed to show up on radar systems.

News.title: 'I'm a qualified mermaid with a pro licence - heatwave means I've never been so busy'
News.content:
'I'm a qualified mermaid with a pro licence - heatwave means I've never been so busy'

Hannah Pearl is a qualified free diver, scuba diver and holder of an official mermaid licence from one of the world's first mermaid schools

View 4 Images Hannah Pearl is a professional mermaid (Image: SWNS)

A qualified 'professional' mermaid has seen her business boom in the heatwave. Hannah Pearl, 44, claims to have been a mermaid since birth and even owns three tails. The mermaid from Bristol is a qualified free diver, scuba diver and holder of an official mermaid licence from one of the world's first mermaid schools in the Philippines.

‌



She is often in the water boasting one of her three colourful mermaid tails, each worth £300. But alongside swimming, Hannah says a big part of being a professional mermaid is conservation work - which for her means educating children on the wonders of the ocean and helping them to protect it.

‌



She has written two eco children's books, volunteers at local libraries for mermaid storytelling sessions, and goes out regularly on beach litter cleans. Hannah, who also crowned Mrs Ocean World UK 2026 at a national pageant centred around conservation and environmental action, said: "I have been a mermaid since I was born - and honestly I always believed I could be one.

‌



"Being underwater is crabulous for me. A huge part of what I do is help children fall in love with the ocean, and make them aware of the incredible marine life that is worth protecting.

View 4 Images Hannah Pearl, at the Festival of Nature in 2025 (Image: SWNS)

"There is no better way for kids to learn than to hear this from someone who is from the ocean. Summer is definitely busier with kids events and parties - many more people are visiting beaches and swimming in the sea due to the heatwaves.

‌



"It's so important to protect our beaches and ensure people take litter home and participate in safe swimming following RNLI advice."

Hannah learnt how to swim at the age of three, and scuba dive when she was 25 in the Great Barrier Reef, in Australia. After falling in love with diving, Hannah attended one of the first 'pioneering mermaid schools in the world ' in 2017 - the Philippine Mermaid Swimming Academy - to obtain her mermaid licence.

Mum sheds more than one third of her bodyweight after daughter's desperate plea READ MORE :

She also attended the UK's first mermaid camp where she learnt how to pose underwater with a mermaid tail, free dive, and how to host mermaid diving parties for kids. She now has three mermaid tails, each costing £300 and made from swimsuit material, and also makes her own mermaid outfits from recycled materials that she collects on litter picks.

‌



Hannah added: "Scuba diving underwater with a mermaid tail is actually quite difficult. But if you ever get to try it I would really recommend."

View 4 Images Hannah Pearl, 44, from Bristol (Image: SWNS)

Her other mermaid duties include passionately spreading the word about our need to protect the ocean. Hannah said: "Children are the future ocean heroes.

‌



"It's about spreading that important message whilst making it fun and engaging. We protect what we love."

Hannah's published children's books are based on a marine warrior mermaid who tackles big marine problems, such as the Great Pacific Garbage patch (a huge collection of marine debris in the North Pacific Ocean) and ghost nets, which threaten the lives of all marine life.

View 4 Images Hannah in the water (Image: SWNS)

‌



She has also released a free online children's game called 'Little Ocean Rescue' - which is raising money for Marine Conservation Society UK, the Paul Watson foundation and the Two Minute Foundation.

Hannah's top eco-tips for how to be more sustainable include talking an extra bag out on a walk to collect any litter you see, get involved with a local beach clean group, stop eating fish and swap out one plastic item per month.

She added: "It's not about being perfect but making small changes and being a conscious consumer!"

News.title: Ramipril and bisoprolol users issued UK government caution relevant this week
News.content:
Ramipril and bisoprolol users issued UK government caution relevant this week

'Essential advice' for millions of us.

View Image (Image: Catherine Delahaye via Getty Images)

Millions of individuals taking commonly-prescribed medications across the UK should take on board "essential advice" from the UK government which is again particularly relevant in the coming days.

‌



Among the medications highlighted by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) are ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers. Numerous other medicines are also referenced by the agency, which are detailed further below.

‌



Ramipril is an ACE inhibitor extensively prescribed to treat high blood pressure and heart failure. Meanwhile, bisoprolol ranks amongst the most frequently-used beta blockers, prescribed to treat angina, high blood pressure and heart failure, amongst other conditions.

‌



On 26 June, the MHRA re-issued guidance on safeguarding your medicines during extreme heat and remaining safe as the UK experienced a heatwave of severe temperatures which peaked at a record 37.7C and resulted in school closures. Temperatures are once more anticipated to exceed 30C in some parts of the UK on Monday and remain in the mid-to-high-20Cs for the rest of the week. This makes proper care and storage of your medication essential once again.

Alison Cave, chief safety officer at the MHRA, stated: "It's easy to forget that medicines left in the heat – in cars, bags, or on sunny windowsills – might not work properly when you need them. Some medicines can also make you more likely to burn in the sun, feel dizzy, or get dehydrated, especially if you're taking diuretics or have a condition like asthma, heart disease, or diabetes."

Why heat affects your medication

The MHRA states that most medicines require storage at temperatures below 25C, a threshold that homes, workplaces, cars and schools have frequently surpassed this summer and may well do again in the coming days.

‌



Heat "breaks down the active ingredients in medicines", the MHRA explains, cautioning that medicines requiring refrigeration "are especially vulnerable to heat". Should medicine be affected by heat, it may no longer function correctly.

How medicine changes how your body copes with heat

While it is widely understood that the body loses greater amounts of water through perspiration in warm conditions, the MHRA notes that "some medicines can make this worse, or make it harder for your body to cope with heat".

It specifically highlights some medicines, saying: "Blood pressure medicines such as ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, or calcium channel blockers can also make it harder for your body to regulate temperature, especially during sudden hot spells. ACE inhibitors can even suppress your natural thirst response."

‌



Frequently prescribed ACE inhibitors in the UK include ramipril, captopril, enalapril and others. Widely used beta-blockers include atenolol, bisoprolol, propranolol and others.

The NHS also highlights important considerations for ramipril users in hot weather, noting that ramipril can cause dizziness, particularly when standing up quickly — a risk that increases in hot conditions due to lower blood pressure and dehydration.

The British Heart Foundation (BHF) also urges heart patients — many of whom are prescribed both ramipril and bisoprolol — to take extra precautions during hot spells. The BHF advises that people with heart conditions are at greater risk of heat-related illness because their cardiovascular systems are already under strain, and that high temperatures can place additional pressure on the heart. The charity specifically recommends that heart patients keep cool indoors during the hottest parts of the day, drink plenty of fluids, and consult their GP or pharmacist if they are concerned about how their medication may be interacting with the heat.

‌



The MHRA also notes that individuals taking the following medications should likewise be mindful of a potentially heightened impact during hot weather:

"Some diabetes medicines, including insulin and metformin, also increase the risk of dehydration or make early symptoms harder to spot."

"Antipsychotic medications, such as olanzapine or quetiapine, or stimulant medications for attention disorders can increase your body temperature, making you overheat more easily."

"People taking diuretics, or ‘water tablets’, such as furosemide, are already losing more fluid through urination."

It further adds that certain common medicines can increase your susceptibility to sunburn, amongst them some antibiotics, diuretics, antidepressants, or skin treatments for acne or eczema.

Article continues below

Signs and symptoms of dehydration

Dehydration can trigger dizziness, headaches, fatigue, confusion, and dark-coloured urine. This poses a particular risk to elderly people, young children, and those with heart or kidney conditions. Should you begin feeling unwell in the heat, move to a cooler location, drink water gradually, and seek medical attention if your condition fails to improve promptly.

News.title: Man finds cat wandering around Alton Towers and is floored by how far he travelled
News.content:
Man finds cat wandering around Alton Towers and is floored by how far he travelled

A man was left gobsmacked when he noticed an adorable black cat wandering through Alton Towers, and when he found out the distance he'd allegedly travelled to be there, he couldn't believe it

View Image The cat was found at Alton Towers (stock image) (Image: Getty)

Alton Towers is a great family day out packed with adrenaline, but one man reportedly got far more when he found a wandering cat, who had travelled very far from home. The last thing you expect to see when you're rollercoaster hopping is a furry friend walking around the park, too, as there's nothing in Alton Towers to entertain a moggy.

‌



But that's exactly what seems to have happened in this case. However, the man didn't realise how far from home he actually was when he sat down and stroked the gorgeous puss.

‌



Coastertog, who shares content from theme parks, explained on Facebook what allegedly happened when Plagg was found.

‌



He penned: "Goodbye, Alton Towers cat. This story is kinda crazy! Yesterday, this loveable fella was taken to the vets by Alton Towers staff, and it turns out he was microchipped and had an owner!

"His name is Plagg, and he had wandered all the way from his home in Cheadle to spend all his time at Alton Towers (sounds a bit like me). Plagg has now been reunited with his family from Cheadle".

‌



Coastetog then urged people to let him know if anyone sees Plagg again, writing: "If you ever see Plagg back at the resort again, please let me know, as staff are worried he may wander back to the park. So goodbye, Plagg, it’s been lovely knowing you, but I’m so happy you’re now safe and back home".

Cheadle, where Plagg is from, is approximately six miles away from Alton Towers, so he's travelled quite far from home.

In the comments, a man shared a similar experience that his grandad had with cats in the past.

‌



One wrote: "There is a good chance Plagg may wander again, as it's a known fact. My grandparents, many years ago, had a cat, and they moved house some three miles away. The cat was named Wisky, and three times my Grandad went in search of Wisky the cat and took him back home to their new home.

"But Wisky had other ideas and again wandered off. After he'd wandered again, my Grandad went in search of Wisky, and sure enough, he was wandering around their old home area.

"My Grandad decided not to take Wisky back to the new home again, but instead looked over the old home garden to see people moving into my Grandad's previous home and decided to speak with the new tenants about Wisky.

Article continues below

"The fact was, Wisky had become content with his old home surroundings and just wouldn't adjust to change. To this day, I never knew what the outcome was for Wisky [...] So if Plagg does return to Alton Towers, it may be for the best just to leave Plagg be to live his cat life as he chooses, and so to avoid any unnecessary unwanted stress".

Someone joked: "That cat would rather be a stray at Alton Towers than live in Cheadle!"

"That's some very typical cat behaviour right there," another said.

News.title: 'Doctors blamed stomach pain on heavy periods - then I was diagnosed with terminal cancer'
News.content:
'Doctors blamed stomach pain on heavy periods - then I was diagnosed with terminal cancer'

Haelwyn had been troubled by stomach pain for years but doctors dismissed it as period pain, stress or IBS - but after a scan to see her unborn child, she was diagnosed with stage 4 cancer

View 4 Images Haelwyn Adams discovered she had terminal cancer after her 20-week scan (Image: Just Giving/ Haelwyn Adams)

An expectant mum whose pleas about stomach pain fell on deaf ears discovered she had terminal cancer.

‌



Haelwyn Adams, 41, was excited to see her unborn child at the 20-week pregnancy scan, but she was still being troubled by pain that had "tormented" her for years.

‌



Writing in The Times, she said: "I'm 41 years old and I'm dying. I don't know how long I've got - a week, a month, a year. Nobody is talking about a decade."

‌



Medics blamed her symptoms on bad period pain, IBS, stress, or, after she and now-husband Luke started IVF, hormonal side-effects as she was young, fit and healthy.

After she became pregnant and suffered another miscarriage, Haelwyn wanted doctors to perform a colonoscopy to explain her pain. But a doctor said she was "simply too young to have colon cancer" and opted for a sigmoidography in just the lower bowel.

When she became pregnant again and felt pain at her 20-week scan, Haelwyn's pain was finally taken seriously.

‌



View 4 Images Haelwyn doesn't know how long she has left (Image: Just Giving/ Haelwyn Adams)

She writes: "On the way to the toilet before we left, another wave of pain threatened to knock me over. My mask of bravery slipped; I leant against the wall, sweat pouring off me, my legs shaking.

"A doctor on the foetal medicine team was walking past and - just like that - I was in a bed and being sent for a scan."

‌



The scan picked up a malignant tumour in her colon with a rare mutation which had already metastasised to her liver.

The mum-to-be was given a choice - abort the baby so doctors could remove the tumour and immediately begin chemotherapy. Or continue with the pregnancy while surgeons remove as much of the primary tumour as possible, which would protect the baby but dramatically reduce her own chances of survival.

View 4 Images The family has set up a JustGiving page (Image: Just Giving/ Haelwyn Adams)

‌



Haelwyn called it "the easiest decision ever". She felt pain whenever her unborn daughter kicked. Eventually, the baby was delivered at 32 weeks as she could hardly breathe with the liver tumours pressing against her lower lung.

Their daughter, Magnolia Sunshine, was born before being immediately separated from her mother.

She said: "From that moment, my days telescoped into a binary routine, by night, journeying into the natal intensive care unit to sit with my daughter, by day, journeying to the edge of my will to live. I had been willing to die for her, but living for her now seemed almost too hard."

‌



The new mum was briefly cancer free in January this year and she hoped the super-aggressive chemo had worked. But it returned with a vengeance in March, with tumours in both sides of her liver, and her treatment is now about management rather than cure.

View 4 Images Haelwyn Adams said continuing with the pregnancy was 'the easiest decision ever' (Image: Just Giving/ Haelwyn Adams)

Her and Luke got married in June, in case she died during an operation to reverse the stoma from the colostomy she had during pregnancy.

Article continues below

She added: "It's hard marrying someone to make them a widower but Luke is the love of my life, my person, my team-mate - and I know how strong he is.

Haelwyn and Luke set up a JustGiving page, hoping to raise £150,000 to "protect my husband and little girl from the financial burden this disease leaves behind". To donate visit here.

News.title: 'I thought my three-year-old had pins and needles - it was actually his eighth stroke'
News.content:
'I thought my three-year-old had pins and needles - it was actually his eighth stroke'

Cat Davies could not understand why her son, Henry, was making a strange noise when he laughed - until doctors diagnosed him

View 3 Images Cat Davies with her partner, Ian, and their son Henry (Image: Cat Davies© SWNS)

A mum who thought her young son had pins and needles or was simply "being silly" was left stunned when doctors revealed he had actually suffered multiple mini strokes. Cat Davies said the first signs were so brief that she never imagined they pointed to a life-threatening condition.

‌



Cat, 38, from Crowthorne, Berkshire, first noticed something was wrong in October 2025 when her son Henry, then aged three, started laughing strangely while playing with his cousin. He also became unsteady on his feet, but the episode lasted only a couple of minutes before he returned to normal.

‌



"I thought it was pins and needles or he was being silly," Cat said. "It only lasted one or two minutes, so I just disregarded it."

‌



Over the following weeks, Henry had one or two more similar episodes, but they disappeared almost as quickly as they began. It wasn't until one evening at bedtime that Cat realised something was seriously wrong.

View 3 Images Cat Davies and her son Henry (Image: Cat Davies© SWNS)

While reading Henry a story, Cat noticed him laughing even though nothing in the book was funny. When he tried to stand up to reach a toy plane hanging from the ceiling, he struggled to keep his balance.

‌



"He was wobbly and he couldn't stand up," she said. "At first I thought maybe it was pins and needles or he was being silly."

Moments later, Cat noticed the right-hand side of Henry's body had become weak and the corner of his mouth had drooped. Unable to speak, he started making unusual grunting noises instead.

"That's when I recognised the signs of stroke," Cat said. "I shouted to my husband, 'I think he's having a stroke.'"

‌



Mum sheds more than one third of her bodyweight after daughter's desperate plea READ MORE :

The couple immediately called 999 before Henry was taken to their local hospital and later transferred to Southampton Hospital. Doctors carried out 23 tests in 24 hours, including MRI scans, blood tests and examinations of his heart.

The results revealed Henry had been experiencing transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs), also known as mini strokes, caused by blood clots in his brain. Cat said she had no idea children could suffer strokes and was shocked by the diagnosis.

"They didn't know what caused them," she said. "I didn't even know children could get strokes, and I have quite a lot of medical knowledge."

‌



A consultant suggested Henry's chickenpox infection six months earlier may have been a possible trigger, although tests found no remaining trace of the virus. Cat said Henry had been due to receive his chickenpox vaccine the same week he was diagnosed.

"You just can't help but think 'what if'," she said. "If we'd just got the vaccine quicker or not taken him to nursery that day, none of this could have happened."

View 3 Images Cat noticed something was wrong with Henry when reading him a book (Image: Ian Davies© SWNS)

‌



Now aged four, Henry has not suffered another stroke since his diagnosis and is due to start school in September. Although scans showed he had experienced eight strokes and sustained some brain damage, Cat said he is currently showing no symptoms.

"You would never know what happened to him," she said. "Right now, he's not presenting any symptoms of brain damage. He's happy and healthy."

The ordeal left both Cat and her husband Ian struggling to come to terms with what had happened. Cat has since undergone counselling and admits she still worries whenever Henry behaves differently.

Article continues below

"Any time he's a bit silly, I just get scared," she said. "Is there going to be another one?"

Wanting to help other families facing similar experiences, Cat decided to write a children's book inspired by Henry's journey after failing to find one that reflected what he had been through. Harry's Wibbly Wobbly Moments has now been self-published, with all profits going to the Stroke Association and the Paediatric Neurology department's Amazon Wishlist.

"I'm not doing this to make money," Cat said. "I just want to help other children like Henry."

News.title: Three killed after bomb detonated at Moscow restaurant, state media say
News.content:
At least three people have been killed and 21 injured after a homemade explosive device was detonated at an Italian restaurant in Moscow, Russian state media reports, quoting security officials.

The blast happened at about 20:00 local time (17:00 GMT) on Kudrinskaya square near the city centre.

The National Anti-Terrorist Committee said a woman carrying the explosives tried to enter the restaurant but was stopped by a security guard.

The device detonated, killing the woman, the guard and a visitor to the Balzi Rossi restaurant, which had been holding a private function.

Authorities have not said who they believe was the target, but many Muscovites will suspect a link to the war in Ukraine.

In recent years, several senior Russian military figures have been assassinated in and around the Russian capital. Moscow has blamed Kyiv for those attacks.

Initial reports said the blast happened in the establishment's kitchen but the restaurant later issued a statement saying "there was a problem outside".

The restaurant is located in one of Moscow's famous Stalin-era skyscrapers, with roads around the square briefly closed.

Dozens of cyclists had been gathering nearby for an evening ride through the city but the event was cancelled.

Video released by Russia's RIA news agency showed heavily armed law enforcement officers at the scene, which had been closed off to members of the public.
