"Canada's next submarine fleet will secure our coastlines and waters," Prime Minister Mark Carney said early last month in announcing the choice of Germany's ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems as the preferred bidder for the country's new underwater fleet.

Patrolling Canada's three coasts will be part of the job for the fleet of up to a dozen state-of-the-art diesel-electric 212CD submarines, says retired vice-admiral Darren Hawco, who commanded Canada's Atlantic Fleet and served as the nation's military representative to NATO until 2020.

"With three oceans, the Arctic responsibilities, they're one of those strategic assets that we want to have."

But Hawco says the subs — which are intended to replace the navy's aging Victoria Class fleet and could be ready by 2034 — will also travel the world.

He expects to see them used in global hot spots from the Taiwan Strait and the nine-dash line in the South China Sea to the Mediterranean and the Baltic.

Protecting the seabed and everything on it

Nearer to home, the subs' job will include protecting underwater infrastructure and resources that many Canadians are only dimly aware of, like the fibre-optic cables that carry trans-oceanic communications.

"Most people do not appreciate that 90 per cent of global telecommunications actually runs across the seabed," said retired vice-admiral Mark Norman, former commander of the navy. "Everybody thinks it's satellite based."

"In the early days of the [current] Ukrainian conflict, we saw the vulnerability of underwater infrastructure."

Even for these more domestic tasks, the submarines' range of 7,000 nautical miles (13,000 kilometres) will be needed "because the distances are so vast," said Norman.

The new subs "have lots of endurance. They are not designed to go anywhere particularly quickly, but they are designed to stay at sea for relatively long periods of time, get into a patrol area, and basically stay there."

Their air-independent propulsion lets them remain submerged for about three weeks, allowing them to operate invisibly in areas such as the eastern and western approaches to Canada's Arctic coast and archipelago.

A scale model of the TKMS 212CD submarine at the Canadian Association of Defence and Security Industries annual defence industry trade show CANSEC, in Ottawa, on May 27. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Riches under the sea

Hawco says the immediate threat in the North is the fact that Canada and Russia have overlapping undersea claims.

There would be little return for Russia to invade Canada's Arctic archipelago, much less its mainland, he said. But the ocean floor is a different matter.

"I think the return for them is to say, 'I own the entire Lomonosov Ridge and all the resources that are there, and there's nothing you can do,'" he said, referring to the 1,800-kilometre-long ridge under the Arctic Ocean that's the subject of a territorial dispute.

The answer to that kind of threat, Hawco said, is "having a submarine that can operate at that kind of distance, that's covert, super-quiet and can sink anything that comes close."

WATCH | Canadian submarine torpedoes decommissioned ship off Hawaii: Canadian submarine torpedoes decommissioned ship off Hawaii | Duration 0:56 As part of a bi-annual exercise, Canada's HMCS Corner Brook torpedoed and sank a decommissioned American vessel, a former guided missile cruiser called the USS Mobile Bay, on July 12.

As undersea mining becomes more important, said Hawco, the subs will be called on to make sure resources on Canada's continental shelf aren't pilfered.

He cites reports on the amount of rare earth minerals Japan has found by surfacing mud offshore. "That's just an indication of how much unexplored, unidentified and unarguably unexploited critical minerals there are in seabeds," he said.

Protecting those resources in the future will involve submarines and a major investment in undersea technology, including "a whole bunch of sensors, whether sitting on the bottom or mobile," Norman said.

A needle in a haystack

A major role for the submarines in NATO's new Cold War with Russia and other adversaries will be intelligence-gathering and surveillance, including the covert insertion of special forces troops.

"They could be trailing other platforms, be they surface ships or submarines. They could just be doing general surveillance, including surveillance of land-based targets," said Norman.

Norman says he sees the subs working in concert with a fleet of underwater drones, and doesn't believe drones will render the submarines obsolete. Instead, their stealth will keep them relevant.

"Technology is not going to solve this problem in our lifetimes. It still will continue to be like finding a needle in a haystack, and nobody's figured out how to do that yet," Norman said.

Stephen Fuhr, secretary of state for defence procurement, speaks on his phone at CFB Esquimalt on Vancouver Island following an announcement July 6 about TKMS's winning bid to supply the Royal Canadian Navy with a fleet of submarines. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

Fear of what lurks in the deep

That stealth is the key difference between the new submarines and the current Canadian fleet.

"It's hard to hide on this globe today with space surveillance being what it is," said Hawco. But the new submarines "are able to operate in a very dead zone of water where sound doesn't propagate well."

The goal is to create a mystery about where they're deployed.

"One of the greatest challenges in naval operations for an adversary is the knowledge that a submarine is out there somewhere, but you don't know where," said Norman.

When a Canadian frigate begins a deployment, there is typically a sendoff with fanfare. Pictures of the mission are posted to a Facebook page or the DND website and the frigate can be followed through online ship trackers.

Canada's new underwater fleet will be much more secretive.

A submarine "could be just sitting on the seabed off its own home port," said Norman, "but it doesn't matter because it's the fact that it's at sea," and therefore invisible. "It becomes an asymmetric consumer of resources to try to find a submarine.

"When you have a larger fleet, which we're hoping to get, it has a multiplication effect on an adversary. If they know that Canada has six submarines deployed at a particular moment, in a crisis, then where the hell are the submarines?"

Canada skips chance to get strategic weapon

Canada's choice of the German 212CD submarine over the larger South Korean Hanwha KSS-III wasn't a purely technical decision, but also took into account economic and strategic factors, including the Carney government's desire to integrate into European supply chains.

In an active war, the classic role of the submarine is to hunt and sink enemy shipping. The 212CD can accomplish that either with torpedoes or by launching cruise missiles through its torpedo tubes, which break the water's surface to strike a ship or a target on land. The subs will likely use a yet-to-be-developed supersonic cruise missile with a range of about 800 kilometres.

But in rejecting the Hanwha option, Canada also turned down what would have been its first real strategic weapon — one powerful enough to change the whole war calculus for a potential adversary.

One difference between the two subs is the South Korean one's ability to vertically launch ballistic missiles — in its case, the Hyunmoo-4 — a capability normally seen in nuclear-powered submarines.

WATCH | Carney announces Canada to buy up to 12 submarines from German shipbuilder: Canada to buy 'up to 12' submarines from German shipbuilder | Duration 1:14 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is negotiating to procure 'up to 12' submarines from German shipbuilder Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems. Speaking to reporters in Halifax on Monday, Carney called the reported $24-billion procurement the 'largest in Canadian history.'

While the Hyunmoo-4 may not ultimately exceed the 212CD's cruise missile in range, it is a true ballistic missile that reaches into the exosphere and comes down at 10 times the speed of sound, making it very difficult to stop.

Moreover, its warhead weighs two tons, or about 15 times as much as the cruise missiles proposed for the TKMS submarine, and a sub in the Gulf of Finland could strike Moscow.

In fact, the KSS-III and Hyunmoo-4 package looks very much like a submarine designed in a country that's thinking about nuclear weapons.

In Canada's current strategic situation, Hawco said, it expects to fight as part of the NATO alliance, and "the military expectations of NATO for Canada don't today include such a capability."

"It would have been transformational in some respects from a war-fighting perspective," said Norman about the South Korean option. "But that doesn't mean the absence of that capability is in and of itself a vulnerability or a problem."

In a different future, though, in which NATO and NORAD might continue to fray and Canada finds itself more alone, the choice to forego a strategic weapon might come to be regretted.

"There's no denying that we won't have that capability," said Norman. "And I can't sit here and tell you categorically that not having it is not a problem. But we didn't specify it as a mandatory requirement."

World.title: The man who phoned in Canada's most famous UFO sighting became the face of the mystery
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As 17-year-old Laurie Wickens drove some friends home from a dance on a clear October 1967 night, he spotted lights in the sky.

As he travelled on Highway 3 in an isolated, coastal part of southwestern Nova Scotia, he saw four lights in the sky that flashed in sequence, then all together at the same time.

All of a sudden, the object crashed into the waters off the fishing village of Shag Harbour.

Wickens drove to a phone booth and called the RCMP. He was initially met with skepticism and was asked if he'd been drinking. Shortly after the call ended, the payphone started ringing.

"When he answered, it was the RCMP," said his daughter, Stephanie Wickens. "And they're like, 'Mr. Wickens, stay where you're at. We've got officers coming because we've just got more phone calls.' He said, 'I told you I wasn't lying.'"

In what came to be known as the Shag Harbour UFO incident, Wickens became its public face. It was a role that continued until his recent death at 76.

This CBC News footage shows the search in the days following the Oct. 4, 1967, Shag Harbour UFO incident. (CBC)

The Oct. 4, 1967, event is considered Canada's most famous UFO incident, said UFO researcher Chris Styles, who has written books on the topic — in part because of the large witness pool, what authorities said at the time, and the subsequent paper trail left behind.

"I don't think we'd all be talking about this today to the extent we do if it wasn't for Laurie Wickens," Styles said.

The Shag Harbour UFO Incident attracted coast-to-coast attention, as evidenced by this Oct. 7, 1967, cover of the Nanaimo Daily Free Press. (Newspapers.com)

One of the RCMP officers who responded, Const. Ron O'Brien, described seeing a light floating about 800 metres offshore.

"It was being carried out to sea by the tide and disappeared before we could get a boat to it," he was quoted as saying by The Canadian Press.

Styles said RCMP officers commandeered two fishing boats to see what was in the water and if there were any survivors, assuming a plane had crashed. They were joined on the boats by local fishermen and other residents, including Wickens.

"When they go out upon the water, they find a trail of odd yellow foam that's bubbling to the surface … some say it smelled of sulphur," said Styles, noting the foam was described as being 24 metres wide and 800 metres long.

He said depending on who you talk to, the object either disappeared or submerged.

No planes were reported to be operating in the area at the time of the incident, Styles said.

The day after the incident, Thursday, Oct. 5, the search continued. Archived CBC News footage of the day shows Wickens was part of it.

Laurie Wickens, right, is shown with an RCMP officer on Oct. 5, 1967. Other footage gathered shows him on a boat with RCMP as they search the waters off Shag Harbour. (CBC)

On Friday, Oct. 6, a naval diving team was brought in, and seven divers searched through the weekend.

The Canadian Press reported the depth of the water searched ranged from nine metres to 20 metres, and "visibility was good over a flat sand sea bottom."

"They claimed to find nothing, although some local residents claimed — and it was recorded in the weekly papers — that some debris was brought up," said Styles.

The investigation reached the highest levels of National Defence.

An Oct. 6, 1967, memo by Col. W.W. Turner, the director of operations at National Defence headquarters, noted "The Rescue Co-ordination Centre conducted [a] preliminary investigation and discounted the possibilities that the sighting was produced by an aircraft, flares, floats, or any other known objects."

Another memo written by Turner later referred to the sighting as an unidentified flying object , but that does not mean its origins were extraterrestrial.

Styles said UFO researchers often call the events of Oct. 4, 1967, "The Night of the UFOs" because there were multiple sightings in Nova Scotia, including in Wedgeport, Sambro and Halifax, but what happened in Shag Harbour eclipsed the others. (Styles said he saw an orange orb over Halifax harbour that same night.)

Stephanie Wickens said her dad wasn't always comfortable telling his story.

"Some people were like, 'Oh, that didn't happen. It's not true,' even though there was so many witnesses," she said. "And I think he just kind of got out of [telling] it."

An Oct. 6, 1967, memo by a National Defence official describes some of the details surrounding the Shag Harbour UFO incident. (Public Archives Canada)

When she was growing up, her dad was vague about what he saw. But when she was around 16, she remembers being at the family's hunting camp when he finally shared his story.

"For a long time when I was little, he'd be like, 'Oh, it was a plane crash,' but then as I got older, he's like, 'I don't know what it was,'" said Stephanie Wickens.

Laurie Wickens spent much of his working life in the fishing industry, mostly as a fisherman.

In his later years, he was heavily involved with the Shag Harbour UFO Incident Society, the non-profit that runs a museum and an annual UFO conference.

The post office in Shag Harbour, N.S., had its own postmark honouring the Shag Harbour UFO incident, as shown in this file photo. (CBC)

She said her dad could come across as gruff, but had a heart of gold and would make friends wherever he went.

Stephanie Wickens said her father would often get calls from strangers when the museum was closed or during the off-season.

"He'd be like, 'Yeah, give me five minutes,' and he'd go open it up for them," she said.

In 2018, the Royal Canadian Mint started a coin series called Canada's Unexplained Phenomena. The first was for the Falcon Lake incident in Manitoba.

Souvenirs are displayed at the Shag Harbour UFO Interpretive Centre in Shag Harbour, N.S., in 2017. (Andrew Vaughan/The Canadian Press)

Styles said Wickens contacted the mint and told them they needed to do a coin for Shag Harbour, which was released in 2019.

Styles first interviewed Wickens as a researcher, but the pair grew to become close friends. He said Wickens saw the Shag Harbour incident as an important part of the community's history.

"His effort was to make it a living, breathing thing again, that people would drive down there and they'd let the story seep into their bones," said Styles.

"And I think he accomplished that in spades."

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Ships stranded in Gulf could pose global invasive-species threat, study says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ships stalled in the Gulf region because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz could trigger a "super-spreader" event, with long-term environmental consequences, according to a paper published last week.

The paper, published July 22 in Biological Invasions, warns that algae, barnacles, tunicates and other organisms growing on stationary vessels in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman could pose an "immense international biosecurity threat" once the ships resume travelling.

"If you had to design a biofoulic spreader event and you really wanted to get as many species moved around as possible, this would be it," said lead author Mario Tamburri, a professor at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science.

The Strait of Hormuz lies between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. There are over 1,500 ships stalled due to the closure of the Strait as a part of the U.S.-Iran war, researchers estimate. (The National/CBC)

The researchers estimate about 1,500 ships are stalled in the Persian Gulf and hundreds more in the Gulf of Oman because of the strait's closure amid the U.S.-Iran war.

Biofouling — the accumulation of organisms on ships hulls, propellers and other external surfaces — could allow invasive species to spread to ports around the world if the vessels are not properly managed, the paper says.

Why the ships could become 'super-spreaders'

Tamburri and his co-authors describe the closure as a "worst-case scenario."

Ships generally remain in port for one to three days and may go years between hull cleanings. Some vessels in the Gulf have been stationary for at least 40 times as long as usual, the researchers said.

Hull coatings designed to prevent biofouling also become less effective when ships remain idle, Tamburri said.

WATCH | Canadian ships stuck in Strait for months: 2 Canadian freight ships stuck in Strait of Hormuz for months | Duration 5:48 Pascal Larose is the vice-president of Desgagnés, a shipping company that has had two vessels stuck in the Strait of Hormuz since hostilities between the U.S., Israel and Iran broke out. Larose says it's uncertain when the ships will be able to complete their voyages.

The number and size of the vessels, their proximity to one another and the timing of the closure increase the risk of a "super-spreader" situation, Tamburri said. The ships became stranded as waters were warming and many organisms were beginning their growing and reproductive seasons.

Species that tolerate the Persian Gulf's high temperatures and salinity may also be effective invaders elsewhere, particularly as ocean temperatures rise, Tamburri said.

Cleaning the vessels before they leave would be difficult. In-water cleaning companies are not equipped to handle so many ships in a short time period, he said, and sending workers into the water during a conflict would pose safety risks.

"Ideally they would all clean before they left, but most of these ships are just going to have to leave," he said.

Shipping's ecological issue

Species can move between ecosystems through cargo and ballast water, but researchers say biofouling has received less attention.

After zebra mussels appeared in the Great Lakes in the mid-1980s, governments and the shipping industry focused on species transported in ballast water, said Meghan Mathieson, director of strategy and engagement for ClearSeas, a non-profit aiming to raise awareness about marine shipping.

"There just was less awareness of the fact that organisms can cling to the outside of a ship and then drop off in new systems," she said.

The N.W.T. will be getting a boat washing station similar to this one installed next spring. It's part of an effort to stop invasive species like zebra mussels from entering the territory. ( Invasive Species Centre)

This zebra mussel was one of 19 pulled off the Mactaquac Dam by Bruce's team during last year's survey of the Saint John River. (Submitted by Meghann Bruce)

Organisms can detach or release larvae when a ship reaches another port. If they become established, they may out-compete native species.

Tunicates, or sea squirts, are one example. The slimy invertebrates, which spread through biofouling and ballast water, compete with mussels on farms along Canada's East Coast.

The International Marine Organization released an updated set of guidelines around biofouling in 2023. Unlike for ballast treatment, Mathieson said there are no mandatory regulations yet but they are in the works.

WATCH | East coast shellfish face tunicate invasion: Slimy and spreading fast: Shellfish farms face biofouling 'invasion' | Duration 3:02 Scientists are monitoring dozens of sites in Nova Scotia and southern New Brunswick to see if the latest warm winter in Atlantic Canada accelerated the spread of slimy biofouling marine invertebrates. Paul Withers has the story.

Such species are nearly impossible to eliminate once established, said Anthony Ricciardi, a biology professor and director of McGill University's Bieler School of the Environment.

"There's a chronic cost to having an invasion once it's entrenched," he said.

Ecological invasion

Ricciardi compared marine invasions to a hub-and-spoke network: Ships carry organisms to ports, that may become new hubs for further spread.

With so many vessels stalled in the Gulf, he said, they are likely to collect an "abundance and diversity" of organisms, increasing the risk of invasions elsewhere.

The situation shows how geopolitical events can have ecological consequences far beyond the region where they occur, he said.

The scale and impact of any spread remain unknown.

"What happens in the Strait of Hormuz will probably fuel a legacy that will keep unfolding," Ricciardi said. "You have to look at it as not just a one-off, but as a major step change in the marine invasion risk worldwide, at least in areas that can accommodate these particular species."

World.title: On Ukraine's front lines, female soldiers testing Canadian-designed body armour
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian soldiers fighting on the front lines of Russia's war are now testing curved body armour designed specifically for women so they're better protected against bullets, shrapnel and drone strikes.

Ukrainian MP Iryna Nykorak said the majority of the more than 10,000 women serving in combat in her country are wearing ballistic plates for men that are too bulky, heavy and don't fit their chests. Some decide not to wear the plate at all, which makes it useless, she said.

"Right now, women must adapt to the current system, not vice versa," Nykorak told CBC News. "It's a respect to women's dignity.... She left her home, her family, sometimes in the majority of cases children, and joined the army. She sacrificed a lot."

Many countries around the world, including Ukraine and Canada, issue servicewomen standard body armour that isn't shaped specifically for them. Last month, Ukraine started handing out its first round of female body armour vests, saying there's a need for this protective equipment as the number of women serving grows.

In June, the U.K. also separately donated 2,000 sets of body armour to Ukraine that include curved female-specific ballistic plates by Canadian company NP Aerospace, paired with vest carriers designed by Logistik Unicorp, also based in Canada.

More than 75,000 women are serving in Ukraine's military, including more than 10,000 in combat roles on the front lines, according to Ukrainian MP Iryna Nykorak. (John Moore/Getty Images)

CBC News spoke to a female officer with the National Guard of Ukraine who's been serving for almost 15 years and is being identified only by her call sign, "Kudriava," in accordance with Ukrainian military rules.

She served in major combat operations across eastern Ukraine, including Bakhmut, Sievierodonetsk, Lysychansk, Chasiv Yar, and the Serebryansky Forest. Today her role on the front lines includes managing drones, electronic co-ordination and signal jamming.

Kudriava said she was on duty in eastern Ukraine when Russia invaded its neighbour on Feb. 24, 2022, and she wore standard body armour designed for men for the first year of the war.

"I have a typical body like slim man," she said. "But a lot of women have a different type of body, and it was hard to do something in the front line when your uniform and your armour are not for you — if you have a big chest, big hips or other types of body."

Kudriava says body armour should fit like a 'second skin.' If it doesn't, it leaves vital areas like the chest and torso exposed, which could be deadly. (Serhii Moos/CBC)

Kudriava started sourcing her own uniform and body armour over the years so that it's more comfortable during her operations, but she said it isn't ideal.

Military gear should fit like a "second skin," she said, and if it's uncomfortable, soldiers can become distracted instead of focusing on their mission.

"When you're in operation and you have some tasks [from] your commander, you shouldn't think about your uniform, you should think to save your life, to save life of your personnel and to do best in this operation," she said.

'Women are not just small men'

Michael Sandercott, part of a team at the NP Aerospace factory in Coventry, England, where the armour is manufactured, said women often size up so that men's body armour fits their breast tissue. This burdens them with extra weight they don't need, so they may give up other items like ammunition, water and rations, he said.

Flat ballistic plates rest again female soldiers' chests, causing the plate to angle outward creating gaps near the neck and lower torso.

"You're much more exposed to the risk of being struck with top-down munitions," he said. "A bullet or shrapnel or anything along those lines. You're less covered."

Erin Grieve, left, a sales manager at NP Aerospace, holds a standard flat ballistic plate for men to her chest to show the gap that it creates. (Lyzaville Sale/CBC)

Erin Grieve, a sales manager for the company's personal protection team, said that "women are not just small men" and body armour shouldn't shrink to fit them. It should be designed to accommodate their breast shape to protect the organs they need to survive.

"You've got your heart, greater vessels, liver and spleen," she said. "So if you were to take an impact, you've got less than 20 minutes to get to a hospital. So what body armour is designed to do is make sure the impact doesn't happen in the first place."

Grieve said her company's ballistic testing and research show that its curved body armour fits tighter to women's bodies, providing better protection.

"So our modelling shows that wearing a curved plate, you are 48 per cent more protected than a flat plate," she said. "So in Ukraine, for example, where you've got drone threats and elevation threats, that gap is really significant."

Grieve shows how her company's curved ballistic plates are shaped to fit a woman's chest, so it's tighter and there isn't a gap exposing vital organs. (Lyzaville Sale/CBC)

MP leads charge for female body armour

Ukrainian MP Iryna Nykorak has spent years pushing for change. She founded Arm Women Now, an NGO supported by NATO that has provided 350 sets of female body armour with lightweight plates to servicewomen. She's also been donating uniforms, boots and gear to fit woman in the battlefield.

"Despite the fact that at the state level they don't have female body armour which will protect their body, their health and their lives, we support them," Nykorak said.

In 2024, Ukraine started giving women jackets and pants for the spring and summer designed for their bodies, she said. But Nykorak said dozens of other pieces of the uniform are not yet tailored to women's bodies.

Ukrainian officials said in July that women are performing in combat missions on an equal footing with men, so it's consistently implementing female-specific protective equipment.

Nykorak said she hopes her country's efforts to get combat soldiers gear that properly fits will lead to other allies, including the European Union, Canada and the U.K., following suit.

"Our experience teaches us a very important lesson that women's participation today is a matter of national resilience," she said. "So it affects a country's ability to defend itself and to survive."

Canada's Department of National Defence said last year it's working on releasing its first body armour system, with darting around the chest, shorter plates and tapering for women, this year for the army's light forces.

Plans are also underway, Canadian officials said, to procure more female-specific personal protective equipment.

World.title: As Trump rolls back endangered species protection, experts say Canadian wildlife is also at risk
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian conservationists and wildlife experts are raising alarm after U.S. President Donald Trump's administration moved in July to weaken habitat protections for endangered species.

The U.S. Department of the Interior announced July 10 that it was rescinding a decades-old definition of "harm" under the country's Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Wildlife and environmental groups immediately condemned the decision, saying it ignores the ecosystems vulnerable species depend on amid widespread biodiversity loss and industrial pressures.

Nearly a dozen groups have filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court challenging the repeal, which takes effect on September 14.

Canadian experts told CBC News the change could threaten animals that spend time in both countries, including species that cross the border to find food, lay eggs, or escape Canadian winters.

Those species include migratory birds, northern spotted owls, grizzly bears and southern resident killer whales, or orcas, said Torrance Coste, the B.C.-based associate director of the Wilderness Committee advocacy group.

"There are no border crossings in [the orcas's] habitat. They just swim back and forth between U.S. waters and Canadian waters and they don't know the difference," Coste said.

"The U.S. lowering their bar, changing the definition of what harm is to an endangered species ... it's a huge concern for us."

WATCH | The fight to protect marine life in B.C.'s Salish Sea: Whales vs. massive ships: making B.C.’s Salish Sea safer for marine life | Duration 4:37 B.C.’s Salish Sea is home to a variety of marine mammals, including the critically endangered southern resident killer whale. For The National, CBC’s Caroline Barghout takes a closer look at the fight to protect marine life in one of North America’s busiest shipping corridors.

How was 'harm' defined?

The Trump administration said rescinding the definition would "end years of federal overreach."

It said Endangered Species Act protections would remain in place while reducing "burdens for landowners and communities."

For decades, U.S. agencies interpreted "harm" to include acts that kill or injure wildlife through significant habitat changes or degradation. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld that interpretation in the mid-1990s.

The repeal "fundamentally undercuts how we've been protecting species for the last 50 years," said Noah Greenwald, endangered species co-director at the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the groups suing the government.

When U.S. habitats decline, Greenwald told CBC News, "that is absolutely going to affect wildlife populations in Canada."

Trump's administration has defended rescinding the definition of 'harm' under the Endangered Species Act. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

Habitat destruction driving biodiversity loss

Protecting animals is "virtually impossible" if they spend months each year in places where habitat protections have been weakened, said Dennis Murray, a Trent University biology professor and wildlife conservation expert.

Habitat destruction is the leading driver of biodiversity loss worldwide, he said. Some species depend on specific plants or ecosystems, including monarch butterflies, which need milkweed to lay eggs and feed their larvae.

Despite that, Murray said, the idea that wildlife protection does not extend across an animal's entire "home range" has been gaining momentum.

"We wouldn't necessarily be content if a fire went through and our house burnt down, but our bedroom remained intact, right? We need the house," he said.

"Likewise, wildlife need their home ranges and the larger area that they occupy, rather than just protecting the individual itself or its nest site."

Monarch butterflies need milkweed plants to lay their eggs. (Gregory Mitchell/Environment and Climate Change Canada)

Concerns in Canada, too

Although Trump's environmental policies are particularly concerning to Canadian conservationists, experts CBC News spoke to warned that Canada may also be moving in the wrong direction.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is seeking to streamline and accelerate permitting for major infrastructure projects amid U.S. tariffs and other economic pressures.

A recent discussion paper on possible legislative and regulatory changes says the government is considering whether to grant the Governor in Council "limited power, with a high threshold to be met, to exempt specific projects from the application of the jeopardy test for species at risk."

"But only if it's in the public interest and if the proponent has made all reasonable efforts to avoid or reduce impacts on at-risk species," the paper says.

Coste called the prospect "very alarming."

Both countries "need to be adding protections and increasing and strengthening laws to protect species, and both again seem to be going in the opposite direction," he said.

Pierre Cuguen, a spokesperson for the Privy Council Office, told CBC News the discussion paper is seeking feedback " to improve the efficiency and predictability of federal regulatory processes" but "does not represent final government decisions."

"Existing requirements to avoid, minimize, and mitigate environmental impacts would continue to play a central role in project planning and decision-making," Cuguen said in an emailed statement.

"Any future changes would need to strike an appropriate balance between protecting Canada's environment and enabling major projects to proceed in a timely and predictable manner."

Environment and Climate Change Canada also said conservation and nature protection are a priority for the government, pointing to a $3.8-billion federal nature strategy announced in March.

In an email to CBC News, a spokesperson also said the department has a "longstanding relationship" with the U.S. under a trilateral committee on wildlife and ecosystem conservation in North America.

Canada "will continue to work alongside our partners in all available capacities to protect nature and species," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Evacuations underway as fast-growing wildfires threaten communities in B.C.'s Interior
World.content:

Evacuations are underway around two fast-growing wildfires in B.C.’s Interior, one near the Okanagan Lake and another in the East Kootenay.

Two separate evacuation orders have been issued as the out-of-control Bradley Creek wildfire threatens communities around the northern end of Okanagan Lake near Vernon, B.C.

The Okanagan Indian Band ordered residents in the Head of the Lake area and other properties threatened by the Bradley Creek fire to leave immediately Saturday evening.

The order applies to residents north of Bonneau Road and south of Highway 97, those along Head of the Lake and Hawhola roads, and properties extending to the boundary of Okanagan Indian Band IR No. 1.

The red area northwest of Okanagan Lake shows the evacuation order issued by the Regional District of North Okanagan, while the yellow areas nearby show its evacuation alerts. The larger red- and yellow-shaded areas around the northern end of the lake were issued by the Okanagan Indian Band. (Regional District of North Okanagan)

The band has not said how many properties are covered by its order. It's registered population is over 2,600.

A B.C. emergency alert said the fire was creating a significant risk to life. People north of the fire were directed to head toward Kal Tire Place in Vernon, while those south of the fire were told to head to the Westbank Lions Community Centre in West Kelowna.

The Regional District of North Okanagan issued a separate evacuation order at around 5:45 p.m. for nearly 20 addressed properties northeast of the lake. The district said everyone covered by that order must leave immediately.

More than two-dozen other properties in the area are on evacuation alert.

The Bradley Creek wildfire is seen from Highway 97 near Vernon, B.C., on Saturday. (Jenifer Norwell/CBC)

The Township of Spallumcheen, just north of the Okanagan Lake, has also issued an evacuation order due to the wildfire Saturday night. Residents in the area between Highway 97, Grandview Flats Road and Otter Lake Road are being told to leave immediately.

The township has also introduced Stage 3 water restrictions to preserve water for firefighting. It warned that embers have been carried into other parts of Spallumcheen and urged residents to watch for spot fires.

Westside Road is closed in both directions between Barcelona Drive and Fred Road due to the wildfire.

The out of control Bradley Creek wildfire has grown to more than 10 square kilometres (1,047 hectares) since it was discovered on Friday.

The B.C. Wildfire Service said winds gusting up to 70 km/h pushed the fire east toward Westside Road and Okanagan Lake.

Ground crews and helicopters are working the fire, but the wildfire service said boaters have been getting too close to aircraft collecting water from Okanagan Lake. It is urging people to clear the area and remain close to shore when firefighting aircraft are operating.

New fire threatens properties near Kimberley

In southeastern B.C., a newly discovered wildfire just east of Kimberley has prompted tactical evacuations and highway closures in southeastern B.C.

The Wait Creek wildfire was discovered Saturday morning and had grown to 160 hectares by the evening. It has been designated as a wildfire of note.

The fire is burning between Kimberley and Ta Ta Creek.

Smoke from the Wait Creek wildfire rises east of Kimberley, B.C., on Aug. 1, 2026. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

The Regional District of East Kootenay said officials were going door to door and directing residents closest to the fire in the Ta Ta Creek neighbourhood to leave immediately.

A tactical evacuation is used when an immediate threat to life leaves no time to prepare or issue written warnings.

B.C. Wildfire Service says the fire was burning at Rank 4, involving vigorous surface fire burning at a moderate to fast rate of spread.

World.title: Colombia Reports and 21st-century fascism
World.content:
The coming four years will probably be the toughest yet and I will need your support to keep Colombia’s longest-living news source alive.

The Espriella administration will be the third far-right government I have reported on since I started Colombia Reports in 2008.

I expect the incoming government to be the worst because it seeks to undo socio-economic policies that pulled 4 million people out of poverty and end peace processes that kept us safe.

Independent journalists (and the New York Times) have criticized Abelardo de la Espriella for his ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC and drug traffickers, and his alleged corruption of the judicial system, specifically in Colombia.

Many of these journalists have been harassed by De la Espriella’s law firm through at least 109 frivolous lawsuits, and the publication of their private information.

I can only guess what’s ahead for us after De la Espriella appointed reported frauds as his spokespersons and put a conspiracy theorist in charge of my visa.

I will need your support as what’s coming is probably going to be expensive. The last time I reported on a far-right government, I was forced to spend months in my native country, the Netherlands.

If you are not yet a paid subscriber, please become one. If you don’t want to commit to a monthly contribution, please make a one-time donation.

I promise I will continue reporting on Colombia and will update you on the political situation in Colombia through my podcasts with Richard McColl of Colombia Calling.

World.title: De la Espriella desists from holding swearing-in ceremony at military base
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella has apparently given up trying to be sworn in before the military and asked Congress to allow the ceremony to take place in Cali, Colombia’s third largest city.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said Sunday that volcanic activity made travel to Popayan, the capital of Cauca, made a “secure, well-organized” inauguration ceremony all but impossible.

“For this reason, I respectfully ask the honorable House of Representatives, which has not yet debated my inauguration in a plenary session, to convene the August 7th session in the city of Cali,” said the president-elect.

“As soon as I am sworn in as president of the republic, my government’s first security council will be held in the Marco Fidel Suarez airbase in the city of Cali,” added De la Espriella, suggesting he has given up his aspiration to be sworn in inside a military base.

In an interview, Santiago de Cali University president Carlos Andres Perez, told Blu Radio on Tuesday that Valle del Cauca Governor Dilian Francisca Toro told him the university theater would be used for the inauguration.

Following the main ceremony, De la Espriella will travel to the Pichincha Military Canton, the base of the 3rd Division, to assume his role as supreme commander of the armed forces.

The apparent decision to desist from a military inauguration comes after major tensions with the outgoing government of President Gustavo Petro, who ordered the military not to cooperate with his elected successor.

An inauguration at a military base was also opposed by the Democratic Center, the largest political party in De la Espriella’s far-right congressional coalition.

The opponents claimed that Colombia’s constitution submits the armed forces to civilian authority. A swearing-in ceremony before them would have been confusing and inappropriate.

According to De la Espriella, his intention meant to stress his support for the Colombia’s “heroes.”

World.title: Colombia’s “Shield of the Americas” to operate from Medellin: De la Espriella
World.content:
Medellin will be the home of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” security program, according to Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and Mayor Federico Gutierrez.

At a meeting with authorities from the Antioquia province, De la Espriella and Gutierrez agreed that Colombia’s second largest city is the “head of the snake of drug trafficking and organized crime.”

From Medellin, the metropolitan area, most orders are sent out to the rest of the country. So we’re going to focus our efforts on Medellin to fight crime. Abelardo de la Espriella

The announcement followed alleged calls between De la Espriella, US President Donald Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and meetings between incoming Defense Minister Jorge Mora and the US’ Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph Humire.

Following the meeting, Mora and Humire announced “Plan Patriota 2.0” and the creation of a “Regional Training Center against Drug Trafficking and Transnational Threats,” which would be “aimed at improving interoperability, operational readiness, and cooperation with allied countries” from the Americas.

During these meetings, the parties explored the joint development of a new bilateral program for cooperation and strategic assistance with a regional scope, known as Plan Patriota 2.0. This initiative is conceived as part of Colombia’s accession to the American Coalition Against the Cartels and is based on the design of the new Policy on Defense, Security, and Civic Coexistence, as well as on the strategy for military and police campaigns in priority areas for the restoration and stabilization of security. Jorge Mora

Plan Patriota was a US-backed military strategy that was implemented by former President Alvaro Uribe between 2003 and 2006.

The plan sought to dismantle the military organization of the now-defunct FARC guerrilla group, which it largely did while also killing thousands and forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands civilians.

De la Espriella has said that he seeks to restart Plan Colombia and seek to militarily destroy groups that were formed during and after peace processes with the FARC and the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

World.title: “Water will run out:” Colombia declares emergency over upcoming El Niño
World.content:
Colombia’s government agreed to declare a national emergency over the consequences of El Niño, a climate phenomenon that is expected to bring extreme drought in December.

According to the government’s environmental institute, IDEAM, this year’s Niño could become the worst since the 1950’s and will peak between November 2026 an March 2027.

During a minister’s council, President Gustavo Petro said that excessive heat and water shortages could lead to energy shortages in regions that rely on hydroelectric dams for their electricity.

Petro asked Finance Minister German Avila to transfer COP4 trillion ($1.2 billion) to disaster management agency UNGRD to double the purchase of solar panels to lessen the demand on these hydroelectric dams.

In December last year, the UNGRD already signed a COP4.2 trillion deal with electricity firm Gecelca to buy solar panels.

In order to maintain food production, the president ordered the purchase of desalination plants for the Caribbean region.

Water is what’s going to run out—we don’t know to what extent, but hopefully Bogotá won’t have to suffer through this again. So, any drinking water supply project that’s already been designed but lacks funding must be funded. Drinking water—all the desalination plants we can bring in, because we don’t build them in Colombia — in all the towns in the northern Caribbean. President Gustavo Petro

Last but not least, Petro urged the Justice Ministry to secure “the accelerated surrender of lands, 500 thousand hectares, that have not been awarded” to landless farmers.

“Provide more land and more water to grow food, grow more food in Colombia, because the sun is going to scorch a lot of food and burn crops. And so it’s likely that we’ll be able to make up for the loss in food supply over these six months with new food supplies,” said the president.

Petro urged his ministers to be careful of corruption, which sank the UNGRD in a crisis in early 2024 and resulted in the detentions of multiple government officials.

World.title: De la Espriella denied aspired control over Colombia’s Congress
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress denied control over the legislative agenda to President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and voted for a president loyal to former President Alvaro Uribe.

De la Espriella proposed his friend, Senator Alfredo Deluque of the U Party, to assume the leadership of the Senate, which would have given the government control over the congressional agenda.

Ahead of the vote, eight parties expressed their support for Deluque’s candidacy, which would have given him a 55-vote majority in the anonymous vote.

Former President Alvaro Uribe, whose Democratic Center party would be granted the presidency, accused “Abelardo’s circle” of trying to “get rid of this party” and vowed to “defend ourselves.”

Uribe had put up Democratic Center Senator Honorio Henriquez for the job and ordered his 17 senators to stick to their original vote.

If the Tiger roars to destroy the Democratic Center, we’ll have to become hardworking bees and defend ourselves, just like bees do when they’re attacked… I’m frightened by the idea circulating among De La Espriella’s inner circle of destroying that party. Former President Alvaro Uribe

The former president got the support of President Gustavo Petro, arguably Abelardo’s biggest political enemy.

At a rally that was held ahead of the vote, Petro warned senators of his leftist Historic Pact party “not to vote for fascism.”

Under the leadership of Senate bench leader Ivan Cepeda, who lost the presidential election to De la Espriella last month, all 26 of the pact’s senators voted for Henriquez.

Enjoying the secrecy of their vote, dissidents from the parties who were ordered to vote Deluque also turned on the president-elect and delivered Henrique 56 votes. Deluque ended up with only 45.

Less than three weeks before taking office, De la Espriella lost the loyalty of its largest coalition partner in Congress and will have to negotiate his agenda with them.

World.title: Petro calls for “peaceful resistance” against Colombia’s incoming “viceroyalty”
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro called on the people to “prepare peaceful resistance” to the “viceroyalty” that “has been imposed as the president of Colombia.”

During an Independence Day speech in the poor south of Bogota, Petro told thousands of supporters that “the next president of Colombia will be a servant to the rulers of the United States who helped him ‘get elected’.”

“We move from the status of a republic to the status of a viceroyalty again, just like 216 years ago,” said Petro, who on Sunday accepted to become the political leader of the leftist opposition.

It is time to give the second cry of independence… Shout freedom and resistance! Gustavo Petro

Rather than a repetition of the 1810 revolution, the outgoing president proposed to “prepare for peaceful resistance” in defense of communities who benefited from the government’s reforms.

How do you repeal the decree on hourly work that ends the labor reform that created stability, a vital wage, and better working conditions? How? Well, with a permanent general strike of millions of working men and women in Colombia! It is not just by shouting, it is not just by raising flags, they are already used to that… No, it is with a production strike, which is permitted by the National Constitution of Colombia, it is a universal right! And that indeed is civil disobedience! If they are going to strike down the stabilities, the working conditions achieved in this government, a general and indefinite strike in Colombia! Gustavo Petro

Petro threatened to “surround the centers of illegitimate power in Colombia until legitimacy exists once again, which can only be achieved through free popular decision without algorithms, and without foreign money.”

To protect the people, the president suggested the creation of unarmed “liberatory guards” that work in a network, “because they want to kill.”

Wherever they touch a neighborhood, wherever they touch a peasant estate, the network must summon solidarity, it must become a demonstration of all adjacent neighborhoods, of all adjacent villages, of the whole country if necessary. Gustavo Petro

“The only way to stop fascism,” said Petro, “is in peace. It is with joy, but it is with millions and millions of Colombian men and women.”

World.title: Petro to assume political leadership of Colombia’s leading leftist party
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro said Sunday that he would become the leader of Colombia’s largest political party on the left, the Historic Pact.

In a tweet, Petro responded to Senator Ivan Cepeda, who proposed him as party president at a political rally in the city of Tunja on Saturday.

Petro said he would “accept the proposal of my party after surrendering power to the far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

The president said he would first go “on a vacation I deserve and didn’t have during four years of governance.”

We will work toward peace and social justice and for a national agreement that prevents violent confrontation among Colombians, and we will seek to contribute to the democratic stability of the countries that Simon Bolívar liberated. President Gustavo Petro

The Historic Pact party was formed in March from a coalition of multiple parties that have long supported the political careers of Petro and Cepeda.

Following a significant electoral victory, the party became the largest of Colombia and will assume 25 of 103 seats in the Senate.

Petro’s former party, Colombia Humana, contributed 12 senators to the collective.

The president started his political career while being a member of the M-19 guerrilla group, which demobilized in 1990.

Petro was elected to the House of Representatives in 1998 an became a senator in 2006.

Between 2012 and 2015, the president was mayor of the capital Bogota.

Petro has been the most popular and powerful leftist politician since the violent death of Liberal Party leader Jorge Eliecer Gaitan in 1948, and was sanctioned by the US Government amid his opposition to the genocide in Gaza.

The president has insisted that his successor won the June elections through fraud and has refused to recognize De la Espriella as his successor.

World.title: Colombia’s peace and human rights offices to close: De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Monday that he will close the Peace Commissioner’s Office, which was in charge of negotiating peace and implementing peace deals with illegal armed groups.

“The Office of the Peace Commissioner is coming to an end, because there will be no more sham peace processes during my administration,” said De la Espriella in his weekly address to the nation that was broadcast on his social media platforms.

According to the far-right president-elect, who will take office on August 7, other presidential commissioners that will disappear are those of National Reconciliation. and the Office of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law.

The functions of these offices will be taken over by the Interior, Foreign and Defense ministries that, according to De la Espriella, have been doubling the work of the presidential commissioners.

“These are functions that, by law, are already carried out by other ministries,” so the government can “avoid duplication and extra costs,” said the president-elect.

De la Espriella seems keen to abruptly end the peace policy of his predecessor, President Gustavo Petro, for being too lenient to illegal armed groups.

The president-elect also promised to close war crimes tribunal JEP, which has been trying thousands of former guerrillas and former members of the military.

De la Espriella could only do this through legislation that would change the constitution and the international treaties that protect the victims of an armed conflict between the State and the now-defunct guerrilla organization FARC.

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ð½ðððð¢ ððððððð (@nancysinatra)

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.
