World.title: Fire reported at another Wildberries warehouse in Russia
World.content:
A fire broke out at a Wildberries warehouse in Russia's Samara region on Sunday following an attack, the company's press service has said.

 

In a post on Telegram, the Russian online retailer said there were currently no reported casualties and that "logistics chains have been reorganised."

"The receipt of deliveries and dispatch of orders are now being handled at other facilities," it added.

Video footage circulating on social media appears to show a large blaze at the warehouse, with flames engulfing the building and huge plumes of black smoke billowing into the sky.

In July, Ukrainian forces targeted multiple Wildberries logistics facilities across Russia as part of Kyiv's "long-range sanctions" against Moscow, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the warehouses were involved in supplying drone parts and navigation equipment for the Russian military.

Wildberries was founded in 2004 by Russian billionaire Tatyana Kim and has gone on to become the country's largest online marketplace. Products offered on its website now include items such as knives, helmets, camouflage, and night-vision devices.

Russian strikes on Ukraine

In a social media post on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russian forces had launched around 1,900 drones, roughly 1,600 aerial bombs, and 144 missiles against 16 regions of Ukraine this week.

"Today, Sumy was struck by aerial bombs. In Brovary, one person was killed in a drone strike, and six people were injured," he wrote.

The Ukrainian air force said Russia attacked Ukraine with 133 drones and loitering munitions overnight.

Firefighters put out a fire at a major book warehouse following Russian drone strikes in Kharkiv, Ukraine, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

"According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 am, air defences had shot down or neutralised 109 enemy UAVs of the Shahed, Gerber, and Italmas types, ‘Banderole’ loitering munitions and other types of drones in the north, south and east of the country," the air force said in a statement.

Ukrainian forces carried out their own strikes overnight, targeting the Saratov oil refinery and Engels military air base, per Zelenskyy. An oil depot in the Kaluga region and a facility involved in the storage of attack drones in Brysansk were also hit, he added.

Zelenskyy renews calls for Patriot missiles

It comes as the Ukrainian leader made a fresh plea for more Patriot interceptors.

The US-made Patriot is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against ballistic and cruise missiles, loitering munitions, and aircraft. The coveted system is expensive and limited in supply, but it is seen by Kyiv as crucial to success in its fight against Russian President Vladimir Putin's invading forces.

"The world has Patriot missiles," Zelenskyy said on Saturday evening. "What matters now is for our partners to make the political decision to provide the necessary packages. The United States knows what we need. Europe knows what we need. Anti-ballistic missiles must protect people – not sit in stockpiles."

On Friday, US President Donald Trump appeared to go back on a promise to let Kyiv build its own Patriot missiles.

"We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away that kind of technology," Trump said during a cabinet meeting - despite having told Zelenskyy at the 2026 NATO summit in Turkey that Washington would give Ukraine a license to build Patriots.

"We'll show them how to do it," Trump said at the summit in July, adding: "This way you can't complain that we're not giving them enough."

World.title: AI-generated label becomes mandatory in the EU for companies
World.content:
Deepfakes and other AI-generated content must be labelled from Sunday, as the European Union's sweeping artificial intelligence transparency rules kick in.

 

The goal? To make sure Europeans immediately know whether the online content they see is real or fake.

The EU's comprehensive AI law enters into force in stages. From Sunday, companies must ensure their AI systems like chatbots make it clear to users they are AI, or when an image or text has been created using AI, there must be a label saying so.

This can be done by integrating watermarks and other markers to allow the easy detection of AI-generated content. Firms face large fines if they don't comply.

The guideline also states that deployers of AI systems must inform individuals when they are exposed to:

Emotion recognition and biometric categorisation tools

Deepfakes

Text publications on matters of public interest without human review or editorial control

Deepfakes in focus

"Generative AI enables disinformation to be created at unprecedented scale, tailored to specific audiences, and disseminated with remarkable speed," an EU official said.

Since AI is "making it increasingly difficult for all of us to distinguish what is real from what is synthetic", the official said, the EU's rules seek to "preserve citizens' ability to trust what they see, hear, and read".

Of particular concern for the EU are deepfakes, text, images, videos and sounds that appear to be real but are generated or manipulated by AI.

The rules affect content made for professional reasons, and the EU insists individuals using AI in a purely personal capacity will not be affected.

Text that aims to inform the public on general interest issues will also have to be labelled if they are created using AI without human editorial oversight.

Existing AI systems have until 2 December 2026 to adapt to the new rules, and there are exemptions for "artistic, creative, satirical, fictional" work.

EU pressures firms

The EU has come under fire for placing more demands on businesses, and rules that will ultimately force all content to be labelled given the rapidly growing widespread use of AI across Europe.

"We have heard that it is going to be very, very difficult to implement. But I think we often hear this with compliance requirements. And yet, the world turns and we figure these things out," said Ashley Casovan of International Association of Privacy Professionals.

The world's tech giants have already begun slapping their own labels in anticipation of the rules.

For example, TikTok has required content creators to label AI-generated images, audio and video for several years, and says over three billion content items already have labels thanks to tools and detection technology.

Likewise, Meta has deployed an "AI Info" label on Instagram and Facebook for posts using the technology.

Google has signed the EU code of conduct on AI transparency, and says it is working with others like Nvidia, OpenAI and Apple on digital tagging tools.

But Google's Karen Massin warns of "regulatory complexity" that could prove counterproductive, and "risks confusing the people these rules are meant to help".

"If online content is flooded with overlapping AI labels and legal disclosures, it becomes harder for people to get the clear context they need," Massin added.

World.title: Cutting sugar up to age two associated with lower dementia risk ‘decades later,’ study finds
World.content:
The research suggests that reducing sugar intake during the earliest stages of life was associated with a lower risk of dementia, a later onset of the disease and better markers of brain health in later life.

 

“Limiting sugar during the earliest stages of life may have lasting benefits for brain health,” said study author Jiazhen Zheng, of The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in Guangzhou, China. “These results highlight the potential importance of early-life nutrition in reducing the risk of dementia decades later.”

Researchers analysed data from nearly 65,000 people born before and after World War II, when the British government introduced sugar rationing across the United Kingdom.

Sugar rationing, introduced during and after the war, ended in 1953. Once restrictions were lifted, average daily sugar consumption nearly doubled, rising from around 41g to 80g.

The researchers grouped participants according to their exposure to sugar rationing: those exposed before birth and during their first year of life, those exposed before birth and up to the age of two, and those born after rationing had ended.

Using medical records from the time participants were around 55 years old, the researchers tracked dementia diagnoses over the following 15 years.

People exposed to sugar rationing before birth and during their first year of life had a 21% lower risk of dementia than those born after sugar rationing ended. Those exposed to rationing before birth and up to the age of two had a 23% lower risk of dementia.

Among people who developed dementia, those exposed to lower sugar levels early in life were diagnosed an average of 2.6 years later than those who were not.

“Sugar restriction in the first 1,000 days was associated with lower dementia hazards, delayed onset, and more favorable brain-health profiles,” researchers wrote, adding that the findings support reducing sugar intake early in life as a potential strategy to lower dementia risk.

“Limiting added sugars during pregnancy and infancy may be one beneficial step that families and communities can take,” Zheng said, while stressing that further research is needed to understand how early-life sugar exposure influences dementia risk.

World.title: 13 dead after Nazca Lines tourist flight crashes in Peru
World.content:
A light aircraft carrying tourists to view Peru's Nazca Lines crashed on Saturday, killing all 13 people on board, according to authorities and local media.

 

The Cessna Caravan C-208 involved in the incident, operated by Peruvian airline Aerodiana, had taken off at around 12:10 pm local time on Saturday from Pisco airport for a sightseeing flight over the world-famous geoglyphs.

"At approximately 1 pm, when the aircraft was flying near the town of Socos, the crew reported an emergency to the Nazca airfield control tower, after which all radio contact was lost," Peru's Ministry of Transport and Communications said in a statement.

Eleven tourists and two pilots were on board when the plane went down. According to the state-owned Peruvian news agency Andina, the passengers included seven Italians, two Germans, and two Spaniards.

"We have information that 11 passengers and two crew members have died," Police Major Jorge Andrade told reporters at the scene of the crash, per AFP.

"Given the severity of the accident, there are no survivors. We have recovered four bodies so far," he added.

Police officers recover the bodies of the victims who died when a sightseeing flight over the Nazca Lines in Peru crashed. Saturday 1 August 2026 AP Photo

Sightseeing flights over the attraction from the nearby airport had already been temporarily suspended on Friday due to wind speeds exceeding 40 kilometres per hour.

The Nazca Lines in southern Peru are a vast collection of geoglyphs etched into the desert floor around 2,000 years ago.

They depict animals, plants, and geometric shapes, among other figures, and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Best viewed from the air, sightseeing flights in small aircraft have become one of the most popular ways for visitors to view the ancient designs.

World.title: Italy brings in border checks for arrivals from Spain: what changes
World.content:
The migration crisis in Ceuta has sparked a political row between Italy and Spain. After news that thousands of migrants had reached the Spanish enclave, Giorgia Meloni's government announced tighter border checks on arrivals by sea and air from Spain.

 

Why people are talking about a suspension of Schengen and what it actually means

Several media outlets on Friday reported that Rome had suspended the Schengen agreement in relation to Spain, because in a post on X Prime Minister Meloni wrote that "the government has decided to temporarily suspend the free movement regime provided for by Schengen on maritime and air links with Spain, reintroducing border checks".

However, the Schengen agreement already allows border controls to be reintroduced "in the event of a serious threat to public order or internal security", a step that Italy has already taken for more than a year at the border with Slovenia for citizens coming from third countries. The measure has been described by Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi as "important but precautionary".

Italy has therefore reintroduced border checks with Spain as an exception to Schengen rules, given that no country can unilaterally suspend another from the free-movement area.

How checks work for travellers arriving from Spain

Minister Piantedosi went on to explain that this is the reinstatement of border controls at sea and air frontiers with Spain for a period of one month and that it is a measure "aimed in particular at monitoring the regularity of movement of non-EU citizens within the Schengen area".

From Saturday morning, airport police carried out random checks at Rome Fiumicino, Milan Malpensa and Milan Linate airports. For EU citizens it was enough to show proof of identity, while non-EU nationals had to present, in addition to an identity document, valid residence permits or visas.

For citizens travelling from Italy to Spain, by contrast, nothing changes and they remain free to enter the country.

The row between Rome and Madrid draws in the EU

Rome's decision to restore checks has prompted a strong backlash from the Spanish authorities. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has sent a letter to European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, calling for intervention from Brussels to support Spain and bring EU countries back into line on strategies to contain the migration crisis.

At the same time, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Danish leader Mette Frederiksen sent a letter to the European authorities, co-signed by 22 leaders of member states, requesting a meeting to discuss urgent measures against irregular migration.

On Saturday afternoon, von der Leyen wrote on social media that she had held talks with Commissioners Brunner and Šuica to discuss the crisis in Ceuta, explaining that most of the migrants who had entered the enclave irregularly had already been repatriated.

The Commission president then added that none of the migrants from Morocco had reached mainland Spain or other EU countries, reiterating the need to strengthen Europe's resilience and saying she was ready to take part in the videoconference requested by European leaders. It will be organised next Tuesday by the current president of the Council of the European Union, Micheál Martin, the Taoiseach of Ireland.

In their letter, Meloni and Frederiksen called for joint action "to strengthen external borders, tackle irregular migration, combat human traffickers, make returns more effective and remove any factor that could encourage new illegal entries".

World.title: Trump says he's cancelling strikes on Iran as 'perimeters of a deal' agreed
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has announced he is cancelling a new attack on Iran after Tehran and a number of unspecified Middle Eastern countries asked the US to postpone strikes as the "perimeters of a deal" had been agreed.

 

"This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.

He added that he had called off strikes subject to "rapidly" making a deal but warned that US forces remained "locked and loaded and ready to go."

"I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," he said, adding: "The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment."

Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency later reported that unnamed Iranian military officials had rejected Trump's claim that Tehran had requested that the US stop the attack, calling it a "new lie" designed to "blackmail Persian Gulf rulers."

They also said that Iranian forces remained "at the highest level of readiness," adding: "If a confrontation becomes inevitable, the battlefield will be decisive."

Trump's announcement came after the US State Department issued a warning to Americans in the Middle East to be on alert amid potential escalation in the region.

"Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions," it said in a security update on Saturday.

On Friday, Trump had said he was "losing faith" in the prospect of a peace deal and threatened to hit Iran "very hard."

Strikes resumed this week

Washington and Tehran have been locked in conflict since late February, when the US and Israel carried out a series of strikes on Iran, prompting the Iranian military to effectively close the Strait of Hormuz - a vital energy transit chokepoint that carries roughly a quarter of the global seaborne oil trade.

Small boats line the shore as cargo ships and other commercial vessels appear anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, July 27, 2026. AP photo

Following a brief pause in the conflict, the US and Iran resumed strikes earlier this week after Tehran launched ballistic missiles against US forces stationed in the Middle East.

Washington hit back by targeting what the US military said were dozens of Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) locations in Iran, including missile and drone facilities and military command centers.

"The strikes aimed to further diminish threats posed by Iran and its proxies to American forces, commercial shipping, and neighboring Gulf countries," US Central Command said.

The two nations had appeared to make progress towards a peace deal in June, with the signing of a "memorandum of understanding." The provisional agreement required an end to hostilities, the US to remove its naval blockade of Iran, and Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and reaffirm that it "shall not procure or develop nuclear weapons".

It gave Washington and Tehran 60 days to achieve a final deal, but ongoing strikes have cast doubt on negotiations over implementing the agreement.

World.title: Explosion in Moscow restaurant killed three and injured 21
World.content:
An explosion Saturday at a Moscow restaurant that killed three people and wounded 21 others was a bombing, Russia's national anti-terrorism committee said.

 

"A homemade explosive device blew up at a restaurant in Kudrinskaya Square in Moscow, killing three people," said the committee, quoted by the Tass state news agency.

The three people killed were a woman carrying the device into the restaurant, a security agent who stopped her and a customer.

Telegram channel Baza, known for its ties with Russian security forces, first talked about a gas explosion that would have come from the restaurant's kitchen.

The restaurant had been booked for a private birthday party and Alexandre Tchaïko, the commander of the Russian Air Force, was present, reports say.

An earlier statement by Moscow police to the Ria Novosti news agency said investigators and police forensic specialists were at the site.

Images posted on Russian Telegram channels showed fire engines and ambulances outside the building.

Several terrorist attacks in past years

Russia has been the target of several terrorist attacks in the past.

Since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, Ukraine's secret service has claimed or been accused of several attacks on Russian military officers and public figures backing the conflict.

Russia blamed Ukraine for the killing of a senior general, Yaroslav Moskalik, in a car bomb in April 2025.

In August 2022, the nationalist Darya Dugina, daughter of hardline Russian ideologue Alexander Dugin, was killed outside Moscow when a bomb attached to her car detonated.

Many believe her father was the intended target.

In April 2023, pro-Kremlin military blogger Vladlen Tatarsky — real name Maxim Fomin — was killed when a statuette he was handed exploded at a cafe in Saint Petersburg.

A bomb attached to a scooter outside a Moscow apartment block killed General Igor Kirillov, head of the Russian army's chemical weapons division, and his assistant in December 2024.

And the pro-Kremlin writer and nationalist Zakhar Prilepin was seriously wounded in a May 2023 car explosion that killed another person near the city of Nizhny Novgorod.

World.title: Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea
World.content:
Intensifying clashes between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea are threatening a crucial trade artery responsible for nearly a third of the world's wheat supply, stoking fears of soaring prices and shortages.

Advertising

Earlier in July, a Russian cruise missile struck the grain carrier Golden Leo, claiming ten lives. This marked the deadliest blow yet in a mounting campaign by both Russian and Ukrainian forces targeting cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

"This is a new development in recent months," claims shipping analyst Yoruk Isik, who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. Isik warns that cargo vessels are caught in a deadly tit-for-tat.

"Ukraine has been targeting Russian seaborne bulkers in particular, the ones transporting stolen grain from the occupied territories of Ukraine," explains Isik, "Russia retaliated and hit Ukraine's civilian port infrastructure in Odesa; a mid-sized vessel carrying corn out of Odesa was totally sunk, other vessels were damaged, and sailors died," he adds.

Turkey’s Shipowners’ Association, having logged 136 incidents involving commercial vessels in recent months, is now urging its members to avoid the Black Sea altogether.

Beyond its role as a key channel for Russian oil, the Black Sea is a lifeline for global grain exports, with Russia and Ukraine among the top suppliers.

"It is very important to note that most of Russia's agricultural commodities are exported through the Black Sea, and that almost all of Ukraine's agricultural commodities are shipped via Ukraine's ports," warns Isik.

Bad timing for harvest

Around a third of the world's wheat moves through these waters. The surge in attacks across the Black Sea and the neighbouring Sea of Azov has brought exports to a near standstill.

"No port is officially closed, but almost no shipowner wants to go there, so trade is close to zero," claims Istanbul-based international grain dealer Can Atbasoglu. "Sellers want buyers to handle the vessels, and buyers want sellers to handle the vessels, but shipowners don't want to risk it."

This deadlock arrives at the worst possible moment: harvest time. "Normally, Russian sellers would have sold all their August cargoes by now; I don't know if anybody has any sales on their books at present," says Atbasoglu.

Turkey agrees deal to clear Black Sea of mines that threaten Ukrainian exports

Wheat prices are already reacting. "The price in Romania is, say, 20-25 percent higher – that's the clearest effect we're seeing. But everybody is waiting for some kind of intervention, and soon," adds Atbasoglu.

Turkey now leads a NATO mission, along with Bulgaria and Romania, to safeguard navigation in the Black Sea. However, former Turkish ambassador and navigation rights expert Mithat Rende believes Ankara will be wary of any effort to enforce passage for commercial ships. "It's very important that the Ukrainian war should not be transformed into a regional war," cautions Rende.

"Where would it stop? Would you fire missiles and intercept Russian missiles in the Black Sea? They (Russia) already accuse all of us of fighting Russia as NATO. It's very important to avoid such operations," he adds.

Full impact yet to be felt

Rende argues Ankara’s priority is diplomacy, having played a pivotal role in brokering the 2022 United Nations-backed grain export deal after Russian forces blocked Ukrainian shipments. "Turkey maintained a dialogue with both the Russian and the Ukrainian sides at the same time," says Rende, "But is there political will for a ceasefire now? I don't see it at present."

Grain trader Atbasoglu warns the full impact of the disruption is not yet reflected in prices. "Buyers are still not fully reacting. It's seen more as an August, or at the latest a September issue, and the markets still want to believe both sides will get together and talk," he says.

However, Atbasoglu cautions that time may be running out. "In 2022, Ukraine was completely closed off, and there was a major panic. We saw the effect: wheat prices jumped 50 percent in 2022, and we could expect something similar if this continues," he concludes.

Africa and the Middle East, which are heavily reliant on Black Sea grain, are beginning to seek pricier alternatives. Europe, too, may soon feel the strain, as drought-hit wheat harvests threaten to push global food prices even higher.

World.title: Poland: Prime Minister Tusk defies anti-Ukrainian violence
World.content:
Anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland is on the rise, with numerous attacks against refugees from the war in Ukraine. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has spoken out against the violence and warned of the danger from Russia.

The Polish leader didn't mince his words. "We must wage a resolute fight against this violence, because thugs, hooligans, and this culture of violence are becoming increasingly brazen and insolent — and also because they have received political support," Donald Tusk said on Tuesday, before a Polish cabinet meeting in Warsaw. The liberal-conservative prime minister said he deplored the fact that "more and more such incidents" are taking place all over Poland.

Tusk's comments came in response to an incident in Wroclaw two days earlier, in which three Polish men brutally beat up a young Ukrainian man and his girlfriend on the street. Cellphone videos show the attackers kicking the Ukrainian man as he lies on the ground. The woman was also hit, sustaining injuries to her neck and ear.

The attack came after an argument in a shop; the attackers took exception to the couple's Ukrainian accents. Polish police acted swiftly: Two of the attackers, both of whom have previous convictions, are already in custody, and a third is being sought.

Tusk warned that such incidents negatively impact Poland's image abroad. The country's reputation was greatly enhanced by its willingness to provide assistanceafter the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine. This could be destroyed, said Tusk, "if we allow thugs, hooligans and common criminals to beat and humiliate people just because they have a slightly different accent."

Mood is turning against Ukrainians

Poland provided military and humanitarian assistance to its neighbor from the very beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It took in more than one million refugees from the war, and around 1.5 million Ukrainians are currently living in Poland. The majority of them work, pay taxes, and contribute to the Polish economy.

Ukrainian refugees in a reception center in the Polish capital, Warsaw in April 2022, two months after the start of the war Image: Attila Husejnow/ZUMA Wire/IMAGO

But four and a half years after the start of the war, the mood in Poland has changed. More and more often, Ukrainians are being verbally and physically attacked in public. Last Wednesday a Polish manager on a construction site in Skawina, near Krakow, was filmed aggressively insulting Ukrainian workers. In another incident on a local train near Warsaw, two drunken men shouted verbal abuse at a Ukrainian passenger. On July 11, a man on a bus in Bielsko-Biala insulted and threatened two Ukrainian girls who were trying to take a selfie. Even schoolchildren, including teenagers at a playground, have fallen victim to the new climate of hate.

According to the police, 180 hate crimes against Ukrainians were recorded in the first six months of this year — a third more than in 2025. And on Friday (31.07.2026) the newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza warned that the internet is full of fake news about crimes Ukrainians are supposed to have committed against Poles.

Award of honorary title considered a provocation

Anti-Ukrainian slogans were already apparent during the presidential election campaign last year. But this May was a big turning point. The Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy prompted outrage in Poland with his decision to award a special unit of the Ukrainian army the honorary title of "Heroes of the UPA."

Poland holds the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) responsible for the mass murder of tens of thousands of Polish civilians in Volhynia between 1943 and 1945. Ukrainians, on the other hand, revere the soldiers of the UPA as heroes in the fight against the Sovietization of their country. Individual UPA units continued to fight against Soviet rule well into the 1950s.

Memorial march in Krakow in July 2026 for victims of the Volhynia massacre committed by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army during WW2 Image: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Along with Polish opposition politicians, Tusk is also critical of Zelenskyy in the row about the UPA. However, he believes that the reactions on both sides are exaggerated and counterproductive. Poland's president Karol Nawrocki revoked the award of Poland's highest order to his Ukrainian counterpart, which had been made in 2023. Zelenskyy returned the award by courier to Warsaw.

Avalanche of hate

These demonstrative gestures by both leaders have set off an avalanche. The Polish internet is flooded with hatred for Ukraine. Przemyslaw Czarnek, the prime ministerial candidate of the leading opposition Law and Justice party (PiS), demanded that all military aid for Ukraine be stopped until Kyiv backs down in the row over the interpretation of history.

Current opinion polls speak for themselves. According to a survey by the CBOS institute, for the first time since the start of the war a majority of respondents (54%) were opposed to taking in more Ukrainian refugees. Only 42% supported maintaining the policy to date. In 2022, at the start of the war, 94% of Poles wanted to offer sanctuary to refugees.

Another poll, by the Opinia24 institute for the weekly newspaper Polityka, found that 44% were against providing further aid to Ukraine, and 41% in favor. 54% of respondents opposed Ukraine joining the EU. Only 33% supported Kyiv's desire to become part of the European Union.

The Ukrainians who were attacked in Wroclaw spoke to the NEXTA Polska news service and urged their fellow countrymen to be careful while in Poland. They advised them to avoid any kind of conflict and to "speak less Ukrainian" in public, as a precaution.

Tusk wants to de-escalate the row with Ukraine

Poland's center-left government under prime minister Donald Tusk has emphatically condemned the anti-Ukrainian attacks. The Polish police and judiciary have also acted swiftly and decisively. After the incident in Wroclaw, Tusk urged President Nawrocki to "break his silence" and condemn the violence. So far, Poland's head of state still has not commented. During the presidential election campaign, Nawrocki, a former boxer, admitted that in his youth he took part in an organized brawl between fans of rival football clubs, violence he described as a form of "noble, masculine combat."

Tusk agrees with the opposition's criticism in the row about the UPA. All the same, he is trying to pour oil on troubled waters. On Wednesday, he met with the Ukrainian president Zelenskyy in private for the first time since the UPA crisis. "We also talked about the security challenges that, unfortunately, affect our people as well: it is important that Ukrainians who have left their homes because of the war and found refuge in Poland feel safe," Zelenskyy wrote afterwards on social media, and thanked Tusk.

Continued support for Ukraine

Polish-Ukrainian cooperation is vital for both countries, as demonstrated by an incident in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday (30.07.2026). During a massive Russian attack on Ukraine, a Russian rocket crossed into Polish airspace, landing in a field near a village around 90 kilometers inside the Polish border. The explosion left a crater ten meters wide.

"I know it's not very popular these days to speak well of Ukraine," Tusk said after visiting the scene. Nonetheless, the Polish leader continued: "Poland's security directly depends on the effective actions of Ukrainian forces, including in the air." Tusk stated: "I know where the enemy stands," and added that, despite protests by the Polish opposition, he remains committed to supplying weapons to Ukraine.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Germany: Islamism and right-wing extremism — a story of mutual radicalization
World.content:
Following the attack on a Berlin Pride festival, the focus in Germany is turning to Islamist terrorism. An expert warns: Looking only at Islamists overlooks the parallels with right-wing extremism.

The terror attack on Berlin's Pride parade has shocked Germany. The perpetrator, 21-year-old Abdul Ballout, was a German national and known to German security forces as an Islamist who had tried to join the "Islamic State" group. He had already been convicted of criminal offences twice, and was awaiting a decision about a possible prison sentence at the time of the attack.

The LGBTQ+ community is not a surprising target, according to Jakob Guhl, a director of policy and research at the London-basedInstitute for Strategic Dialogue who has studied Islamist extremism for many years. "The ideology is deeply homophobic and hostile to the queer community. The 'Islamic State' terror group, when it held territory in its so-called caliphate, executed people it accused of homosexuality," Guhl told DW.

In recent years, there have been several attacks on Pride events, Guhl said: In London, Oslo, Zurich and Vienna.

Was the Berlin Pride attack inevitable? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Parallels between different extremist movements

Guhl has also noticed that Islamist extremism has a close relationship with far-right extremist movements. Both ideologies strengthen each other and profit from one another, he argues: "Both are of the view that peaceful coexistence between Muslims and non-Muslims is impossible."

Young Muslims' experiences of discrimination in Germany, being marginalized, and negative reporting about Islam are cited as proof of the German state's hostility towards Islam, according to Guhl.

"In the view of the Islamist extremists, right-wing extremists are representative of Germans as a whole, and on the other hand the right-wing extremists say that Islamist extremists essentially represent Muslims," Guhl says. "There is an attempt to split society into two camps."

Both ideologies overlap in numerous attitudes: contempt for Western liberal society, the propensity toward conspiracy ideas, mistrust of government institutions, anti-feminist attitudes, and hate of the LGBTQ+ community.

"Their reasons for disliking the LGBTQ+ community do vary. On the one hand, from the religious ideological perspective, they believe it goes against the instructions of God," Guhl explained. "On the far-right extremist side, it mostly stems from a biological-racist perspective that it lowers the birthrate and weakens the health of the nation."

Berlin attack: When deradicalization programs don't work To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Germany, security authorities have for years observed the formation of a new generation of young, violence-prone, far-right extremists who are mobilizing against Pride parades.

In a 2018 study entitled, "Loving hate. Anti-Muslim extremism, radical Islam and the spiral of polarization," Guhl and other authors described the common interest of both ideologies: Social division, itself a breeding ground for extremism.

Fuel for extremism: Hate speech on social media

To combat the proliferation of such ideologies, the authors recommended a tougher approach toward hate speech on social media. They also call upon traditional media to avoid one-sided reporting and finger-pointing, which only fuels the polarization spiral.

According to Guhl, one example of this is the current discussion about the background of the attacker of the Berlin Pride event. "I find the question of the nationality of the perpetrator problematic: You quickly run into the danger of creating a two-tier society between different affiliations. That is counterproductive when it comes to the dynamics of radicalization."

For Guhl, it is also important to keep pointing to what Muslim and non-Muslim communities have in common: "We share many more things than those which divide us."

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Germany: As temperatures rise, so does climate skepticism
World.content:
Some 98% of active climate scientists say climate change is happening, and is man-made. Nonetheless, a new study shows the number of climate-change skeptics in Germany has increased. Why is that?

Climate skeptics are no longer a small but noisy minority. They are now "a mass phenomenon," according to researchers at Flensburg University.

In a study published in the scientific journal Global Environmental Change , authors Katharina Gies and Emanuel Deutschmann reported that between 2022 and 2023 there was a big jump in skeptical attitudes to climate change among the majority of the 3,074 people surveyed. Some 59% said they had more doubts about climate change in 2023 than they had had in the previous year.

The researchers wrote that the respondents' individual economic situations could not be considered the primary explanation for the increase in skepticism. Other factors, they said, were much more decisive: A right-leaning political orientation, distrust of state institutions, and dissatisfaction with democracy.

Social psychologist Marlene Altenmüller said the Flensburg publication is important and fascinating, though she has doubts about its alarming tone. Other studies show that "the number of people who have doubts is still very small," she says. Altenmüller, a junior professor at the Leibniz Institute for Psychology in Trier, conducts research into science reception: How people perceive scientific evidence, and what they think about the scientific system and its researchers.

Altenmüller's research indicates that people in Germany do not have fundamental doubts about scientific evidence. Rather, it varies depending on the topic, and the view the group to which people feel they belong has of the topic.

Extreme heat: Can Europe adapt to climate change? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If a group has doubts about climate change, so do its members

Her work, and that of many other researchers, also shows that politically right-leaning people express more skepticism about climate change.

"If right-wing parties were suddenly to discover that we should in fact take action against climate change, my assumption is that the followers of these parties would also believe in climate change and would support political measures," Altenmüller said.

Nor does she believe that climate skeptics have a different personality structure. Instead, climate skepticism is more likely to be down to the fact that "people orientate themselves according to their group and its identity." The credo for most people is that content is secondary, or, as Altenmüller calls it, "Party over policy."

Underlying this is something psychologists call motivated reception. People always see the world through the lens of their own desires, ideas, values, and political ideologies, and anything that cannot be squared with their own ideas and values tends to be disparaged. Altenmüller's research demonstrates that all of us are predisposed to seeing the world through our own filters.

From climate skepticism to conspiracy theories

Both Altenmüller and the Flensburg researchers emphasize that climate change skepticism comes in different guises. One form is the rejection of climate policy measures. The basis for this may be the assumption that it won't be all that bad, or doubt that human activity is the cause. Another is the belief that all the talk about climate change is simply a con, a conspiracy.

This is the focus of research of Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive science at the universities of Bristol and Potsdam. Among other things, he examines the persistence of misinformation and conspiracy theories, and is interested in the parameters that determine whether people reject or accept scientific proofs, especially in connection with vaccines and climate change. "Certain people are more susceptible to conspiracy theories than others," he said.

The COVID-19 pandemic made this very apparent. Lewandowsky argues that for some people, conspiracy theories that apportion blame for a particular situation provide a welcome opportunity to escape from feelings like fear and loss of control. "That offers some brief psychological comfort to people," Lewandowsky says.

However, he goes on to explain that the comfort they derive from assigning blame does not last long. "There's good evidence to suggest that people who do fall into that rabbit hole over time are suffering," he said. "They're less likely to hold their jobs. They lose social contacts. They become mentally challenged."

How climate change forces Indian farmers to stay single To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why climate skepticism is hardly an issue in India

Climate skepticism and conspiracy theories are mostly a Western phenomenon. Researchers observe them the most in the US, Europe, and Australia. In India and other countries of the global south, climate change is already a question of daily survival, and has been for some time. "In India, a lot of people still suffer from [not] getting access to clean drinking water," says Jagadish Thaker, senior lecturer at the University of Queensland, Australia, and an expert in climate change communication.

For years now, he says, people in the global south have been experiencing first-hand the ways that climate change is exacerbating problems through rising temperatures and extreme weather events.

Consequently, measures to reduce emissions and adapt to changing living conditions are not seen as a matter of political ideology. According to Thaker, people in India are trying to counteract their own vulnerability to climate change while still trying to develop economically.

Countering climate skepticism with respect

Heatwaves and other extreme weather events are a direct threat to human life in Germany, as has become apparent during this summer's heatwaves, which are reported to have killed as many as 10,000 people already.

This is why the authors of the Flensburg study are urging people to take climate change skepticism seriously if they are to successfully anchor climate protection measures in society.

Thaker believes the media plays a decisive role. He believes there is still a general lack of information and understanding of the effects of climate change. "The media coverage of extreme weather events, while it's a lot, it is dramatic, and unfortunately doesn't mention climate change."

Altenmüller says it's important to keep emphasizing that there is a scientific consensus that climate change is anthropogenic, or, caused by human activity. Sometimes, she says, it does matter who says it. Research shows that some scientific disciplines are perceived as more biased than others. Consequently, economists have a better chance of their message reaching a wide audience than sociologists.

Taking the values of people who express skepticism into account could also help to communicate a different point of view to them, says Altenmüller. Communication must emphasize not only the restrictions that need to be imposed through political measures, but also the opportunities arising from this.

People who have themselves experienced extreme weather events probably find it easier to shift their perspective. This is why Lewandowsky is hopeful that the this year's heatwaves and wildfires will make a difference. "At some point, people's personal experiences matter," he says.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: China: Dozens dead in Gansu flash floods
World.content:
Chinese authorities will launch an investigation into the floods, amid warnings of further landslides as the rainy weather continues.

The death toll after a flash flood in the northern Gansu province of China has climbed to 25, according to state media reports.

The flood has left 23 others injured, the ⁠official Xinhua news agency reported on Sunday.

What do we know about the Gansu flash floods?

The Shuangshimen Scenic Area, a popular tourist spot for camping, was hit by a flash flood on July 26, with state media initially reporting 10 deaths and 23 injuries.

The country's national commission for disaster prevention said it would oversee an investigation into the event.

Videos of the flood show a deluge ripping through a valley where several tents and cars were parked.

China has been hit by extreme weather this summer, with flooding affecting various areas in the country Image: Lang Bingbing/Xinhua/IMAGO

Authorities have warned of further landslides, including in ‌Dingxi, ​as heavy downpour continues in the annual flood season.

Beijing and Inner Mongolia also issued weather warnings on Sunday as China's ​weather observatory warned of heavy rain, high winds and thunderstorms across a large stretch of the country from ⁠the southwest ​to the northeast.

Edited by: Rana Taha

World.title: On the front line of Europe's battle against wildfires
World.content:
French firefighters have won out over a massive blaze, with almost 200,000 evacuees returning home. But Europe's climate-fueled wildfire season is far from over.

The signal to move comes suddenly — and within a minute or so the fire truck is full and speeding off into the distance, a cloud of orange dust swirling in its wake. "There's always a bit of adrenaline when you get the call," marine firefighter Julien says. "But we're trained; we're prepared."

Maitre Julien — whom DW can only identity by rank and first name — is part of Marseille-based battalion deployed to France's Gironde region to tackle a wildfire which prompted the largest evacuations in the country since World War II.

Some 264 firefighters were injured in the fight against the Gironde fire, four of whom lost their lives. In nearby towns, French flags still fly at half mast to mark the loss. "It's always on our mind," Lieutenant Damien, another marine firefighter, explains as his team members haul the firehose out behind him.

Firefighters are still tackling a wildfire near Bordeaux Image: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/picture alliance

Big battles on little sleep

Letitia, a firefighter and medic, said she tries to ask how colleagues are feeling "without being too intrusive."

"It's the fatigue above all," she says when asked about the most common problem affecting her colleagues. "They're sleeping very little."

"Do you see all all of that?" Maitre Julien asks, gesturing out the car window as he drives past rows of blackened trees and swathes of scorched earth at the roadside. "All of that's already burned. But you can see small peels of smoke here and there. We absolutely have to extinguish those so fires don't restart."

When Julien pulls up at another hotspot, the risk of flare-ups comes sharply into focus: The air smells burned and a cloud of white smoke fills the sky. Within about 20 minutes, the smoke turns thick and black, and the fire — previously under control — was visible burning bright again through the trees.

No respite for France's firefighters battling wildfires To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Here by the firefighters' side are improvised teams of local volunteers — farmers and tradesmen and women who took it upon themselves to use their tractors or vans or four-by-fours to transport water to firefighters on the front line, and often head into the blazes themselves without proper protective gear or training.

"We're here because we're needed. And because we want to help," Steven Page, one volunteer, told DW. Maitre Julien said they played a "primordial" role, saving firefighters "precious time" in the fight.

Winning a 'David and Goliath' fight, together

At times, firefighters said, this felt like a "David and Goliath" battle. But they came out on top. By Saturday, France's Interior Ministry declared the fire was no longer progressing. Most of the 220,000 evacuees were allowed to return home.

Elsewhere in Europe, the heat of battle is far from over: Wildfires have also been raging in Greece and Spain — other countries are likely to face fires in the coming months too.

That's keeping EU crisis management chief Hadja Lahbib busy. She visited Bordeaux on Thursday, meeting local officials in Ornano fire station's crisis room and learning how they felled trees and vegetation across 150 kilometers (93 miles) of land to create tactical firebreaks and prevent the flames from reaching the city.

Dotted around the green lines on the map representing firebreaks are different European flags: Germany, Slovakia, Portugal, Spain, Belgium, Sweden, Czechia, Switzerland, Turkey — some of the countries that sent firefighting aircraft, firefighting crews, and technical teams through the EU's crisis management mechanism.

Maitre Julien is expecting more fires to flare up in August and September Image: Rosie Birchard/DW

More EU funds to fight climate-fueled fires?

"Climate change isn't knocking at our door. It's here," Lahbib told DW on Thursday. Last year, her team laid out an EU crisis preparedness plan designed to better anticipate and prevent wildfires and other disasters through EU cooperation. "For that we need the means," she said.

"We proposed a budget of €10.7 billion ($12.3 billion), which is an important amount of money, but at the same time, it pays back," she said. "It's better to prevent — to anticipate — then to recover. So I hope that member states will follow our proposal."

EU states pay into a communal seven-year budget for the bloc. Some national governments facing their own financial woes — including Germany — are skeptical about the EU Commission's bid to lock in its biggest-ever global budget.

Lessons for the future

Climate campaigners also accuse the EU of walking back on big green promises as the bloc pursues a red-tape-cutting agenda to better compete with the likes of China and the US.

"This isn't 'just nature.'⁣ Decades of burning coal, oil and gas are making wildfires more frequent and more destructive," Greenpeace wrote in a statement last week.

But ⁣Lahbib gave a cautious response when asked about allegations that EU states were dragging their feet on climate action. "This is not the moment for controversy and so on. This is a moment of solidarity," she said. "We will have the time to draw on the lessons learned."

EU crisis commissioner Hadja Lahbib says the EU needs to put more resources into crisis prevention Image: Rosie Birchard/DW

In Brussels, where a small monitoring and decision team runs a bloc-wide crisis response center, unit chief Maria Zuber is already busy planning.

"We need to think of informing the population," she said. "We need to think of evacuation plans. We need to invest in early warning tools. So all this is something that we we are mapping. I think that is the main challenge — that we need to change our mindset."

Wildfire season far from over

Back in Gironde, Maitre Julien is all too aware of what's ahead. "We know we'll have more intense fires like this one more frequently," he said. Even this year's wildfire season isn't over yet — Julien and his team still have all of August and September to get through.

But for now, there's a moment of reprieve. At a hastily setup command center in Lège-Cap-Ferret, firefighters can get a meal and some rest before heading back home, or out on their next shift. There's little privacy — just rows of camp beds in a sports hall full of people. Outside, some firefighters prefer to lie on the ground in the shade of empty firetrucks.

"It's a little moment of cohesion," Maitre Julien explains as he sips coffee and jokes with volunteers. "We're not with our family, so we make this sort of temporary bubble to stay well. So that it's more like home."

Tessa Walther contributed to this article.

Edited by Ben Knight

World.title: No new Iran strikes for now amid deal hopes — Trump
World.content:
08/01/2026 August 1, 2026 Houthis claim Saudi oil shipments diverted

Yemen's Houthi movement says eight Saudi oil tankers have been pushed off their usual routes as part of a newly declared blockade targeting the kingdom's energy exports.

According to the Iran-backed group, the ships will now have to make the much longer journey around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope to reach Asian markets.

Riyadh has not confirmed that any tankers were diverted.

The Houthis announced the blockade last week, framing it as retaliation for what they describe as years of Saudi pressure on Houthi-held parts of Yemen.

The group controls much of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, after seizing territory in 2014 and setting off a war that drew in a Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognized government.

A major concern for global shipping is the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow passage between Yemen and the Horn of Africa that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

Any serious disruption there would add to pressure on trade routes already affected by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis said they do not intend to levy transit charges on vessels using the strait.

World.title: US: Multiple dead in shooting at In-N-Out Burger in Idaho
World.content:
Multiple people were killed in a shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in southern Idaho. The suspected shooter is dead, police said.

Multiple people were killed and others were injured after a gunman opened fire at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in a city in the northwestern US state of Idaho.

The shooting unfolded near a busy shopping area in Twin Falls where hundreds of people were present, police chief Matthew Hicks said in a news conference.

The suspected shooter was among the dead, Hicks said. Police were still trying to determine the shooter's identity and motive.

Local media broadcast video footage from the scene showing what appeared to be a young man carrying a long gun outside the restaurant that had only been open for a week at the Twin Falls location.

Police to confirm exact number of fatalities

The shooting at the burger chain "resulted in fatalities" but authorities were still working to determine the number of victims, Hicks said.

"We are working to try to ascertain his identity and the motivations behind [the shooting] and we'll be able to figure that out in the next coming days," he said, adding that it was a "very chaotic scene."

Local public radio station KTVB reported that three people were killed and two were injured. A city spokesperson said the number of victims is expected to be higher.

Multiple people hospitalized after shooting at Idaho In-N-Out

Police said multiple people were taken to St. Luke's Magic Valley Medical Center.

Hospital spokesperson Taylor Marschner said in a statement that it was "working closely with law enforcement and emergency responders as they manage the situation."

Twin Falls, a city of about 56,000 people, is about 130 miles (205 kilometers) southeast of Boise and about 75 miles (120 kilometers) north of the Nevada border.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: Hungary to shut sole nuclear plant for first time on Sunday
World.content:
Hungary will shut down the Paks nuclear power plant on Sunday for the first time in its 44-year history, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said.

He made the announcement on social media late Saturday night, saying the decision was taken after a further drop in the Danube's water level.

The plant, located 120 kilometers (74.5 miles) south of the capital, Budapest, uses water from the Danube to cool its reactors. It provides more than 40% of Hungary's electricity generation.

Record-low Danube levels necessitated the shutdown

The Danube has fallen to record-low levels in some areas after months of below-average rainfall and successive heat waves since May.

Hungary's water authority projected that the Danube, which flows from Germany to the Black Sea, would fall further in the coming days.

It measured the Danube's water level in Budapest at 23 centimeters (9 inches) on Wednesday morning, well below the previous record low of 33 centimeters (13 inches) set in 2018.

As a result, output at the Paks nuclear power plant had already been cut earlier in the week and some reactors shut down.

"Due to a further decline in the Danube's water level, the second-to-last generating unit at the Paks nuclear power plant will be shut down at 1:30 a.m. (2330 GMT)," the prime minister said.

"As a result, the plant is now producing only 240 megawatts (of electricity), and tomorrow (on Sunday), for the first time in 44 years, it will be completely shut down," Magyar added.

Hungary's large power users asked to cut power

The surge in imported electricity prices could cost Hungary between 120 billion and 240 billion forints ($315 million to $630 million, €273 million to €546 million), Tisza Party Vice Chairman Mark Radnai said on Facebook.

Magyar warned the Paks plant could remain offline for weeks and said his government would seek voluntary power cuts from large users, in addition to the 240 megawatts already pledged, with penalties for noncompliance.

No significant rain is in the forecast for the next few days and temperatures expected to rise to over 38 degrees Celsius (100 degrees Fahrenheit) across the region Image: Robert Nemeti/Anadolu/picture alliance

A decree would also allow grid operator MAVIR to mandate consumption cuts and temporarily disconnect large users if necessary.

"Households will be the last to face restrictions," Magyar said.
