World.title: The split in Poland’s opposition could help them unseat Tusk’s government [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles If Mateusz Morawiecki cuts his final ties with PiS and forms a new party, it may help broaden the opposition’s appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option. While the strings have not yet been fully cut, Poland’s main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), is splitting in two. A group of 40 MPs led by former Prime Minister (and PiS deputy leader) Mateusz Morawiecki have now formed a separate parliamentary caucus of their own, after last week refusing to sign a pledge of loyalty and quit the association they had formed – as had been demanded by PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 The move means that Morawiecki’s caucus, known as Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), is now the third largest in parliament, while PiS, which is down to 147 MPs, has lost its status as the biggest. For now, most of Morawiecki’s followers officially remain members of the PiS party, a situation that will only change if they either resign or are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks. But unless either or both sides make major concessions, it seems only a matter of time before Development Plus becomes a separate party. A lot of international reporting has suggested that these developments will harm Poland’s right-wing opposition and boost the re-election chances of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s more liberal coalition at next year’s parliamentary elections. In fact, PiS’s split could well help the opposition win a majority. Over the last year, PiS has found itself in an increasingly difficult position. Its support in the polls has fallen below 25%, the party’s lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, combined support for two far-right opposition groups – Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) – has risen to over 20%, threatening PiS’s longstanding dominance on the right. In response, Kaczyński has pushed his party in a more rightward direction, picking a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s prime ministerial candidate in March. That signalled that PiS was aiming to compete head to head with the far right on many issues, taking tougher positions on Ukraine, the EU, migration and climate policy. In many cases, that meant disowning the legacy of the PiS government led by Morawiecki from 2017 to 2023. It also meant that the party was ceding the centre ground, something Morawiecki, who represents the more moderate, technocratic side of PiS, was particularly concerned about (alongside his own waning influence). When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Should Morawiecki now, as expected, launch his own centre-right party, focused on economic development, it would appeal to moderate conservatives who are opposed to the Tusk government but put off by the far right and PiS’s own hardline turn. Inevitably, some of the support for Development Plus would come at the expense of PiS – but not all of it, and possibly not even most of it. An example of something similar happening can be seen elsewhere among the opposition. Until last year, KKP was part of Confederation. However, its leader, Grzegorz Braun, was expelled after announcing a run for the presidency against Confederation’s official candidate, Sławomir Mentzen. In June 2025, KKP formed its own parliamentary caucus. Since then, support for Confederation has remained stable at around 13-14%, while KKP has risen to over 9% in the polls. So, by splitting, the two groups actually increased the size of their potential electorate, with KKP successfully appealing to an even more radical pool of voters than Confederation. It is possible that Morawiecki could do the same in the opposite direction – his new party winning over moderate conservatives while PiS continues to appeal to its most loyal supporters as well as competing with the far right. There certainly seems to be fertile ground for such a party. Regular polling by the state research agency CBOS shows that the proportion of Poles with a negative view of Tusk’s government rose to its joint-highest level this month, at 48%, while only 29% have a positive view. The last time that positive views outnumbered negative ones was in February 2024, the second full month of the current ruling coalition’s time in power. Among those who voted for Tusk and his allies in 2023, dissatisfaction is strongest among moderate conservatives. Both Tusk’s centrist KO and one of his coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), are polling only slightly below the proportion of votes they received in that year (30.7% and 8.6%, respectively). However, the most conservative part of the coalition, the centre-right Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance, has fallen from 14.4% of the vote in 2023 to only around 4-5% today for the two parties that constituted it, Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) and the Polish People’s Party (PSL) (which last year decided to go their separate ways). An IBRiS poll for Polsat News in April this year found that, whereas 84% of KO voters and 57.1% of Left voters have a positive view of Tusk’s government, that figure falls to 42.5% for Third Way voters, a majority of whom (51.6%) have a negative opinion. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 Moderate conservatives’ disillusionment with the government, combined with PiS’s shift away from the centre ground, gives a clear opportunity for Morawiecki. And Tusk’s coalition itself showed in 2023 the advantages for the opposition in offering a broader set of options. While some – in KO in particular – had pushed for centrist and left-wing parties to stand jointly on a single list at that year’s elections, instead they campaigned as three main blocs. That gave voters opposed to the PiS government a genuine choice, and likely played a big part in the record turnout that helped bring Tusk’s coalition to power. It is similarly possible now that a four-branched opposition, ranging from Morawiecki on the centre right, through PiS and Confederation, to Braun on the radical right, could together win a parliamentary majority. Polls currently show those four groups with combined support of around 50% (though polling regarding support for Morawiecki’s prospective party should for now be treated with caution). Jestem dumny z tego, co wspólnie zrobiliśmy dla Polski. I wiem jedno – nasza misja wciąż trwa💪🇵🇱#RozwojPlus pic.twitter.com/xOnxKDoroS — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 31, 2026 However, even if they do win a majority, it is far from certain what would happen then. In 2023, the three opposition blocs were, although standing separately, clearly aligned with one another and focused on removing PiS from power. When they together won a parliamentary majority, it was absolutely clear they would form a coalition government. By contrast, today’s opposition is deeply divided. Confederation and KKP regularly attack PiS. It is not at all clear that Confederation would be willing to form a coalition government with PiS, while Kaczyński has explicitly ruled out working with the pro-Russian, anti-American Braun. Meanwhile, Morawiecki’s split has followed months of bitter infighting within PiS, which has often been carried out in public. The manner in which he and his allies are now departing the party means that relations with PiS are likely to remain difficult. The national-conservative opposition PiS party's newly named candidate for prime minister has made overtures to the far-right Confederation. But he also ruled out Grzegorz Braun, an even more radical far-right figure, serving in a PiS-led government https://t.co/i3zOZJWdUN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 It would therefore be hard for the opposition to form a government, even if they do win a majority. In this situation, the role of President Karol Nawrocki may be vital. Though elected with the support of PiS last year, he was technically an independent and maintained good relations with Confederation and even, to some extent, Braun (who endorsed Nawrocki after being eliminated in the first round). When Morawiecki this week announced the “ten pillars” of Development Plus’s programme, he made clear his loyalty to Nawrocki: the second of those pillars is “respect for the president”. Nie ma silnej Polski bez wielkich ambicji. Nie ma wielkich ambicji bez ludzi, którzy je zdefiniują i będą gotowi wziąć odpowiedzialność za ich realizację. Bezpieczeństwo. Rozwój. Suwerenność. Ambicja. Tożsamość. Patriotyzm. To nie hasła wyborcze, ale fundamenty państwa, które… pic.twitter.com/G0YBbfhLye — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 28, 2026 Many on the right hope that Nawrocki can play a role next year in helping the opposition present a more united front during the election campaign. It is also the president who decides who gets the opportunity to try to form a government after the elections. That role would be of particular significance if, as is very possible, Tusk’s KO emerges as the biggest individual party but the opposition together may be able to form a parliamentary majority. Given that we are still over 14 months away from the elections, and Morawiecki has not even yet officially split from PiS, it is still far too early to make confident predictions. However, while Morawiecki’s likely departure is clearly a personal blow to Kaczyński – and a sign of the 77-year-old’s waning influence over not only the Polish right but even his own party – it may conversely provide a boost to the opposition as a whole. Poland has banned children from using smartphones and other electronic devices in primary schools and kindergartens in a bid to improve their wellbeing and safety. The new legislation, signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki on Thursday, will take effect at the start of the school year on 1 September, but schools will have until the end of 2026 to adjust. Prezydent podpisał nowelizację, która zakazuje korzystania z telefonów komórkowych w przedszkolach i szkołach. (PAP)#PAPInformacje pic.twitter.com/CK7YFU7sru — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 30, 2026 Under the new rules, pupils in primary schools and kindergartens will be prohibited from using smartphones and other electronic devices allowing communication or audio and video recording for the entire school day, including breaks and lessons held outside of school grounds. Schools will be allowed, but not required, to create designated places where pupils’ devices can be stored in a safe way and with respect for their privacy. The law, however, allows for some exceptions. When pupils need a device because of illness, disability or other special needs, school headteachers can permit their use. Phones could also be used in emergencies where there is a direct threat to life, health or property. Furthermore, pupils will be permitted to use mobile phones if a teacher deems them necessary for educational purposes and gives approval. The law also allows secondary schools to introduce bans on smartphone use if they choose, but does not make this compulsory, with such schools retaining autonomy to set their own rules through their statutes. The draft law banning phones from primary schools was first approved by the government in June. It then went to the Sejm, the lower and more powerful chamber of Poland’s parliament, which introduced amendments, including extending the measures to kindergartens. The Sejm then approved the bill in a rare near-unanimous vote, with only some MPs from the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) voting against it. Subsequently, the Senate passed the bill without amendments, sending it to Nawrocki, who could have signed it, vetoed it, or sent it to Poland’s constitutional court for review. Poland’s government has approved a ban on mobile phones in primary schools as well as tougher age-verification requirements for online pornography. Both measures still require parliamentary and presidential approval before becoming law https://t.co/y4Ycf46FQD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 The president ultimately decided to sign the law, with his office noting that the measures aim to “create safer learning conditions” and support the “healthy and responsible” use of digital technologies by pupils. Poland’s education minister Barbara Nowacka said last month that the law would “improve teachers’ power, autonomy and agency, as well as order and digital wellbeing in schools”. She added that, although many schools already have such bans in place, teachers had asked for legal backing to help enforce them. For more on the measures, see our earlier report from when the bill was approved almost unanimously by parliament, with only the far right voting against it https://t.co/9Mx0SfkE5V — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 According to a survey conducted in April by the Polish state research institute CBOS for the Polish Press Agency (PAP), 85% of Poles support a ban on the use of smartphones in primary schools. Poland has been recently stepping up efforts to protect young people from various digital threats. The topic has been a rare area of consensus between the government and Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills. Earlier this month, Nawrocki signed a law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour – known in Polish as “patostreaming”. Another measure approved by the government that is now being considered by parliament is the introduction of stricter age-verification requirements for accessing online pornography. In January, the digital affairs ministry also announced that it hoped to introduce measures blocking children from access to social media. Poland hopes this year to introduce measures preventing children from accessing social media, says the country's digital affairs ministry. It is working on tools that would require platforms to verify the age of users https://t.co/G7qeEl2q9x — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Polish authorities have confirmed that the object that violated Polish airspace and crashed in eastern Poland was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload. He added that a Ukrainian pilot had tracked the missile that later fell on Polish territory but was unable to intercept it. “He turned back 20 seconds before reaching the border,” Tomczyk said, adding that the pilot “could not have flown into” Polish airspace. He is banned from re-entering Poland and the Schengen area for five years. The 34-year-old was charged with promoting Nazism, an offence carrying a maximum sentence of three years in prison, and desecration of a memorial site. “A place that symbolises one of the greatest tragedies in human history requires special respect, and insulting it does not go without consequences,” said the border guard. @PolskaPolicja zatrzymała ob. Kolumbii 🇨🇴, który na terenie Muzeum Auschwitz-Birkenau propagował nazizm i znieważył miejsce pamięci. Komendant #PlacówkaSGwKrakowie wydał wobec cudzoziemca decyzję o zobowiązaniu do powrotu oraz 5-letni zakaz wjazdu do 🇵🇱 i państw strefy Schengen. pic.twitter.com/kzfw1Kzw8w — Straż Graniczna (@Straz_Graniczna) July 30, 2026 Police in Oświęcim, the town where the museum is located, said in mid-July that they had detained a man after being notified by museum guards of a possible offence. A police probe found that the man, who had been living and working in the Wielkopolska province, had “posed for a photo making the Nazi salute” at the museum while visiting it. Prosecutors were informed of the case, police said, adding that the man was subsequently charged with two crimes: public promotion of Nazism and the desecration of a memorial site. He admitted to the offences and voluntarily submitted to his punishment, which consisted of a 2,000 zloty (€464) fine along with a decision for his verdict to be made public, they added. He was then handed over to Poland’s border guard, which decided to deport him and ban him from entering Poland and other Schengen countries for five years. The border guard said that the decision was “immediately enforceable”, and was based on “considerations of security and public order as well as the interests of the Republic of Poland.” It also noted that a court decided to place the man in a facility for foreigners in the city of Przemyśl, where he will await deportation. Earlier this month, prosecutors in Poland indicted an Iranian-born German citizen for making statements denying the Holocaust during a tour of Auschwitz. In 2025, an Israeli teenager who was seen doing a fascist salute at the former German-Nazi camp was fined for propagating Nazism. Auschwitz was first set up by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland in 1940 during World War Two as a camp to house Polish “political” prisoners, before later becoming primarily a site for the murder of Jews. At least 1.3 million victims were transported there, with at least 1.1 million of them killed at the camp. Around one million of those victims were Jews. The second largest group of victims – around 70,000 people – were ethnic Poles. Poland’s government has appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, a professor at Wrocław University of Economics, noted that her appointment signals “a shift” from simple promotional activities to “managing the reputation of our great country”. The move comes as Poland seeks to capitalise on its economic success, including growth in tourism and continued investments. But the government says that current promotion efforts lack a single strategy and are fragmented. Czas na markę Polska! Witamy na pokładzie prof. Barbarę Mróz – Gorgoń 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/PPX2eWTRSm — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 29, 2026 Last year, Poland’s sport and tourism ministry appointed Mróz-Gorgoń, who also advises companies and institutions on branding strategy and founded a think tank dedicated to promoting Poland, to an interministerial team tasked with developing a comprehensive new branding strategy for Poland. The government said, however, that efforts to promote Poland were so far fragmented and lacked a single strategy, which is why it created the post of commissioner for promotion of the Poland brand. As the first specialist to take the position, Mróz-Gorgoń will be tasked with preparing a strategy to build a national brand and help implement it, coordinate activities to help grow tourism, support investments, and improve Poland’s position on the world stage. “We will create one programme resulting in the joint promotion of our country’s brand,” said Tusk. According to the government, this will come at no further cost, but ensure that existing funds will be spent in a more “coherent and effective way”. Mróz-Gorgoń, meanwhile, noted that “the Poland brand is not the property of the government. It is created by entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, local governments and millions of Poles at home and abroad”. Developing this brand “means more investment, recognition of our brands and products abroad, and it also provides greater strength in international relations,” she continued. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 Poland has been one of the world’s fastest-growing economies in recent decades. The growth has coincided with the international expansion of its firms, more foreign investments, and a rapidly expanding tourism sector. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP annually within a decade, from about 5% now, and for Poland to become a leader in the sector in central and eastern Europe. Foreign direct investment in Poland grew from just under 15.5 billion zloty in 2003, a year before the country joined the European Union, to around 61.3 billion zloty last year, according to figures from the National Bank of Poland (NBP). Various state and private companies – such as delivery giant InPost, insurer PZU, and train manufacturer Pesa – are establishing themselves abroad by buying some of their rivals. The international success of some Polish athletes – including football player Robert Lewandowski and tennis star Iga Świątek – has also helped improve Poland’s visibility. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. At 3:46 a.m., before the object could be clearly identified, it disappeared from the radar. An Mi-24 helicopter was then sent to the area of the last radar detection to verify the indications. Its crew located what was believed to be the crash site. W trakcie rosyjskiego zmasowanego ataku rakietowego na zachodnią Ukrainę doszło do naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej. World.title: Record number of Poles opposed to Ukraine’s EU membership
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. Last weekend, three men were filmed violently attacking a Ukrainian woman and her partner outside a shop in Wrocław, apparently because of her accent. Two of the assailants have since been detained by police, while their victims required treatment in hospital. In response, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for Poles to “wage war on violence”, saying that the perpetrators of such acts “have become emboldened precisely because they now have political role models, political patrons, and political support”. World.title: Spaniard Santi Denia Named Coach of the Czech Republic National Team
World.content:
Spanish coach Santi Denia took over the Czech Republic national team on Friday to become the first foreigner in the post.

The Czech soccer association said the 52-year-old signed a two-year contract with an option to be extended by another two years.

Czech football association head David Trunda introduced Denia at a news conference in Prague.

“We greatly appreciate that an expert with such a credit and immense experience at the international level is joining the Czech national team,” Trunda said.



“I’m happy to be here and I’m extremely motivated, because I consider it a great opportunity to lead the Czech national team,” Denia said. “Czech football has a magnificent history and I honestly regard it as a great honor to be here.”

Denia replaced Miroslav Koubek who resigned after the team’s early exit from the World Cup.

Denia was a center-back in Atletico Madrid (1994-2005) and has two games on the national team to his credit.

As coach, he led Spain to gold at the 2024 Paris Olympics. He also claimed the European titles with Spain´s under-17 (2017) and under-19 teams (2019).

He was most recently in charge of Al-Shahania, a club in Qatar.

His first major task in the post will be to face tough opponents in League A of the Nations League. The Czechs open the competition by hosting Croatia on Sept. 26 in a group which also includes England and World Cup champions Spain.

World.title: Czech PM Calls for Closing Schengen to Spain due to Migration Crisis in Ceuta
World.content:
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for temporarily excluding Spain from Schengen due to the migration crisis in Ceuta, where about 49,000 migrants entered uncontrollably from Morocco.

Italy has already suspended Schengen rules in connection with Spain.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for closing the Schengen zone to Spain after a sharp escalation of the migration crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.

According to Babiš, the situation in Ceuta is “absolutely scandalous,” and the cause of the crisis was the overly lenient migration policy of the Spanish authorities.



According to the publication, since Thursday, about 49,000 migrants have entered Ceuta uncontrollably from the territory of Morocco. At least 19 people have died trying to cross the maritime border.

Foreign Minister Petr Macinka (Motorists) described the situation as a serious challenge for the entire Schengen Area but stopped short of calling for Spain’s exclusion, saying he wanted to hear Madrid’s position before drawing conclusions.

What is the Schengen Agreement?

The Schengen Area allows people to travel between 29 European countries without routine passport checks at internal borders.

While border controls are normally abolished, member states can temporarily reinstate them if they believe there is a serious threat to public order or internal security.

Italy does not share a land border with Spain, so the decision to reintroduce border controls for a month will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries.

Where is Ceuta?

Ceuta is an autonomous Spanish city on the northern coast of Africa that borders Morocco.

Spain also controls the nearby city of Melilla. Together, the two enclaves form the European Union’s only land borders with Africa.

Roughly the size of inner Sydney, Ceuta has a population of just over 83,000, according to Spain’s Instituto Nacional de Estadistica. It is home to Christian and Muslim communities, including Spanish and Moroccan residents and cross-border workers.

World.title: Prague’s Online Heat Map Shows Where to Find Water and Shade
World.content:
As another spell of extreme summer heat approaches the Czech Republic, Prague has published an online map showing where residents can cool down, find drinking water or spend time near water.

Temperatures in the capital could reach 38°C, with the hottest conditions expected toward the end of the week.

This map is designed to help people find relief across the city and includes public drinking fountains, misting systems, fountains, wells and locations suitable for swimming or relaxing beside the water.

The project was prepared by the City of Prague in cooperation with the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR Prague) and the municipal technology company Operátor ICT.



The initiative is part of the city’s broader efforts to prepare for more frequent periods of extreme heat. Prague says it is increasingly focusing on measures that can reduce the effects of rising temperatures over the longer term, rather than relying only on temporary interventions.

More trees, water and shade planned

Prague is also looking to incorporate more greenery and water into public spaces as part of new development projects.

The city is supporting measures including new fountains and other water features, green roofs, rainwater collection tanks, climbing plants, permeable surfaces and additional tree planting. The expansion of parks is also among the measures being considered.

Temperatures could approach 40°C

The current heatwave is expected to reach its peak on Friday, when temperatures could climb as high as 39°C in parts of the Czech Republic.

Friday night could also remain exceptionally warm, with overnight temperatures staying above 20°C in some areas.

A temporary change is expected on Saturday, particularly in parts of the country where showers and thunderstorms could bring some relief. The cooler conditions, however, are not expected to last.

At the beginning of next week, temperatures are forecast to rise again, with daytime highs between 32°C and 37°C.

World.title: Canadian International High School in Prague: Your Pathway to Top Universities Worldwide
World.content:
Earning an internationally recognized high school diploma and preparing for admission to top universities no longer requires moving abroad.

Canadian International High School in Prague (CIHS) offers students in Grades 10-12 a fully English-language education based on the Canadian curriculum.

Located in the heart of Prague, CIHS combines the strengths of Canada’s education system with the quality of life and accessibility of the Czech Republic. Students receive a globally recognized diploma while studying in a familiar European environment, avoiding the higher costs and challenges of relocating overseas.

An International Diploma Recognized Worldwide

Graduates earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD), Canada’s official high school credential, recognized in more than 20 countries. The diploma provides access to over 30,000 universities and colleges worldwide, including leading institutions across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Europe.

Unlike the Czech education system, which typically spans 13 years, the Canadian program is completed in 12. As a result, students graduate a year earlier, begin university sooner, and gain an additional advantage as they build their academic and professional future.

Learning the Canadian Way

CIHS delivers its academic program in partnership with Toronto Imperial School, ensuring that students follow authentic Canadian educational standards. Courses are taught using modern curricula, teaching methods, and learning resources aligned with those used in Ontario schools.

English is the language of instruction across all subjects. An international faculty, including teachers from Canada, creates an immersive English-speaking environment that helps students strengthen their academic language skills and confidently transition into universities abroad.

To maintain high academic standards, all teachers undergo a rigorous selection process followed by professional training led by Canadian educators and the school’s academic partners.

Outstanding Value

Tuition is, on average, two to three times lower than at many international schools in Prague while offering an extensive range of included benefits.

Tuition covers:

the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD)

an iPad for both academic and personal use

for both academic and personal use a complete school uniform

an annual gym membership

continuous academic guidance and support

and support educational trips to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany

to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany participation in the Exchange program in the United States.

International Experience Beyond the Classroom

Education at CIHS extends well beyond the classroom. Each semester, students have the opportunity to join educational trips to Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, and other destinations. These experiences include university campus visits, meetings with admissions representatives, and valuable insight into international higher education systems.

Students may also participate in the Exchange USA program, spending one or two semesters at one of 40 partner high schools across the United States. The program offers full immersion in American school life while strengthening English proficiency and developing valuable intercultural experience.

For students planning to continue their education in the U.S., CIHS also offers the opportunity to transfer to an American high school during Grade 12 on an F-1 student visa, complete their final year there, and graduate with a U.S. high school diploma.

A Modern Campus in Central Prague

The school is located in Holešovice, one of Prague’s fastest-growing and most vibrant districts. Its central location makes the campus easily accessible from virtually any part of the city by public transportation, while convenient parking is available for families.

The campus occupies a modern business complex close to parks and the Vltava riverfront, providing an ideal balance between study and recreation. Students also benefit from an on-site cafeteria and access to medical professionals, including general practitioners, dermatologists, immunologists, and allergists. Sports facilities, swimming pools, cafés, and shops are all within walking distance.

Personalized University Preparation

Beginning after Grade 10, students choose one of two academic pathways: Business & Social Science or Engineering, allowing them to focus on subjects aligned with their future university studies.

Throughout the program, experienced teachers and academic advisors provide personalized guidance, helping students develop essential academic skills, explore career options, and build competitive university applications.

Graduate Outcomes

By the time they graduate, CIHS students have gained far more than a high school diploma. They leave with:

the internationally recognized Ontario Secondary School Diploma

strong academic English proficiency

experience studying in an international environment

university admissions guidance

a global network of peers

participation in international educational programs

access to leading universities across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, and beyond.

Canadian International High School in Prague welcomes prospective students and their families to visit the campus, meet the faculty, and learn more about its Canadian curriculum.

It’s an opportunity to experience a truly international education and earn a globally recognized diploma – while staying in the heart of Europe.

World.title: Prague Pride Strengthens Security Measures Following Berlin Attack
World.content:
Security will be tightened at this year’s Prague Pride festival following a deadly attack at a similar event in Berlin.

Czech police are preparing additional measures to protect participants in the week-long festival, which begins Monday.

The measures will also reflect changes to this year’s festival route and venue.

Prague Pride is moving its main festival area from Letná Plain to Štvanice Island. The traditional Saturday parade will also follow a new route, starting in the lower section of Wenceslas Square, continuing through the historic center and ending at Štvanice.



Organizers will begin the parade with a minute of silence on Wenceslas Square to remember the person killed in the Berlin attack.

“Thousands of people standing in silence will be a reminder that we will definitely not remain silent about violence motivated by prejudice,” Prague Pride director Kamila Fröhlichová said.

This year’s Prague Pride will feature more than 100 cultural, educational and social events. Dozens of associations, institutions, companies and individuals will organize programs at venues across the capital.

While many events will focus on the lives and experiences of LGBTQ+ people, the festival will also address wider questions surrounding human rights and civil society. A full program is available on the Prague Pride website.

Prague Pride was first held in August 2011. Its inaugural edition was met with strong opposition from conservative groups and politicians, who described the parade as obscene and accused its organizers of promoting what they called an “ideology of homosexuality.”

Then-President Václav Klaus was among the most prominent critics, arguing that society needed to oppose what he described as the spread of homosexuality.

Protests continued in subsequent years but gradually declined in size and intensity.

World.title: Prague Opens Air-Conditioned Space in City Centre to Help Beat Heat Wave
World.content:
People looking for relief from the heat in central Prague can use the air-conditioned ground floor of the Škoda Palace in Jungmannova Street on Thursday and Friday.

The city has opened the space to the public as temperatures across the Czech Republic are expected to rise well above 30°C. The building will be accessible from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on both days.

Visitors can sit on benches and chairs, refill their water bottles at drinking fountains and use the toilets. Drinks and snacks are also available for purchase.



The measure comes as the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute has warned of very high temperatures in parts of the country. Forecasters are advising people to drink regularly, stay out of direct sunlight where possible and avoid strenuous physical activity, particularly during the afternoon.

The Czech Republic is facing several days of intense heat, with Friday expected to be among the hottest day of the current spell. Temperatures above 35°C are possible in some areas.

Individual Prague districts are taking similar steps. Prague 3, for example, plans to make air-conditioned areas in its town hall, information centre and Žižkostel available to the public when temperatures are forecast to exceed 35°C. Visitors will be able to sit down, drink water and take a break from the heat.

The city says the cooling spaces are intended to provide temporary relief during the hottest periods, particularly for people who may struggle to cope with high temperatures.

World.title: Revolut Opens Private Market Funds to Czech Investors
World.content:
Revolut is expanding its investment services in the Czech Republic, giving retail customers access to funds focused on private equity, private credit and infrastructure.

The new products will become available in the Revolut app from July 31. The fintech has signed distribution agreements with four major asset managers — Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane and Partners Group — which collectively manage more than $2.8 trillion in assets.

The move gives Czech retail investors access to parts of the private markets that have traditionally been aimed largely at institutional investors.



Private market investments have often required substantial minimum commitments, frequently above €100,000, or around CZK 2.5 million. Revolut’s new offering is designed to lower that barrier and allow customers to add private assets to portfolios that may already include stocks, bonds and exchange-traded funds.

Investments will be available directly through the Revolut app.

The funds will be offered through the European Long-Term Investment Fund framework, known as ELTIF 2.0.

How ELTIF 2.0 works

The structure is intended to provide investors with greater flexibility than traditional private equity funds, where capital can remain committed for several years and withdrawals may not be possible during that period.

The products offered through Revolut use an “evergreen” structure. This allows investors to put money into funds with existing portfolios rather than waiting for a traditional investment cycle to begin.

ELTIF 2.0 also provides scheduled liquidity windows during which investors can request the redemption of their holdings, subject to the conditions of the individual fund.

That does not mean the investments are as liquid as publicly traded shares. Private market assets remain difficult to sell quickly, and investors should expect to hold their money for the long term.

Revolut already offers Czech customers access to a range of traditional investments, including US and European stocks, ETFs, bonds and commodities. The addition of private market funds expands the investment options available through the same app.

World.title: From Old Town to Main Station: Tourist Charged €150 for Short Taxi Ride
World.content:
A tourist has reported an alleged taxi scam in Prague, claiming that a journey from Old Town Square to Prague Main Railway Station ended with an unexpectedly high fare and a disputed payment.

The incident reportedly took place on July 25 at around 16:15. According to the complaint, the driver charged CZK 980 for the ride, an amount the passenger said was far higher than the expected price for such a short distance.

The tourist claims that the driver refused to accept payment by card and requested cash instead.



“I paid him 100 Euros for the fare. He just took the note, swapped it and lied to me saying what I gave was 100 in Czech currency, and demanded me to pay the remaining 50 euro taxi fare,” the tourist said in his complaint.

“So I paid the initial 100 euro that was swapped, plus the 50 euro taxi fare.”

According to the passenger, the total amount paid for the ride was therefore €150 (over 3,600 CZK). He said he was rushing to catch a train to Bratislava and was unable to resolve the dispute at the scene.

The tourist also claimed that no receipt was provided after the payment. According to his account, the driver said an invoice would be sent by email, but it was never received.

The case has been reported to the relevant authorities, while details of the incident have also been shared online to raise awareness among other visitors.

Travellers are also encouraged to use established taxi applications or services recommended by hotels, restaurants, and official tourist information centres. Paying by card and confirming the expected price in advance can help avoid disputes.

World.title: Péter Magyar: Paks Nuclear Power Plant to shut down completely
World.content:
The penultimate generating unit at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant was taken offline at 1.30 AM on Sunday due to the continued fall in the Danube’s water level, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on his Facebook page late on Saturday night.

The power plant is generating a fraction of its capacity

Prime Minister Péter Magyar highlighted that the plant is now generating only 240 megawatts and that “tomorrow, for the first time in 44 years, it will be shut down completely.” Under normal operating conditions, the Paks Nuclear Power Plant has a generating capacity of 2,000 megawatts.

Earlier on Saturday, Péter Magyar said that, due to the significant reduction in Hungary’s power generation capacity, the Hungarian Independent Transmission Operator (MAVIR) had activated its emergency protocol for major disruptions to the electricity system.

He stated that all available reserve power plants across Hungary were in operation or on standby, including facilities that had long been out of service and were in extremely poor condition. All power plants capable of being brought online have been supplied with the necessary fuel.

Péter Magyar: Large consumers that fail to meet their commitments may face sanctions

Under a government decree that entered into force on Saturday evening, major industrial electricity consumers may be disconnected from the power grid if they fail to implement the required reductions in electricity consumption. Prime Minister Péter Magyar said:

“Households are at the very end of the restriction chain. The burden will first be borne by the state, large corporations, industrial facilities and institutions with deferrable energy consumption. The system operator may only interfere with the electricity supply of Hungarian households once every other option has been exhausted. This is what systemic change looks like in practice.”

As part of the government’s energy-saving measures, rail freight services will be suspended during the most critical period between 5 PM and 10 PM from Monday onwards. In addition, remote working will be introduced for the first three days of next week across all public administration roles where the continuous delivery of services allows.

Those able to work remotely are asked to do so

The government has also called on private-sector companies and employers to allow employees whose work can be carried out remotely to work from home over the coming days, while reducing energy consumption in office buildings to the lowest practicable level.

Péter Magyar also announced that decorative and non-essential lighting at all state institutions will be switched off, and that all local authorities across Hungary are expected to implement the highest possible level of energy-saving measures.

Stay up-to-date: Slovakian PM Fico offers to help Hungary with electricity as Paks shutdown threatens energy supply

Dunamenti Power Plant back in operation

Thanks to rapid repair work, the Dunamenti Power Plant in Százhalombatta resumed operations after three days, the Prime Minister announced on his Facebook page on Saturday afternoon. Péter Magyar noted that this adds a further 360 megawatts of generating capacity to the system and thanked everyone involved in the repair work.

In a statement posted on social media on Saturday, the Dunamenti Power Plant said that, following the successful completion of technical inspections and trial operation, the plant’s G3 generating unit resumed full-capacity operation at 4.45 PM on 1 August. As a result, nearly 400 megawatts of generating capacity has once again become available to Hungary’s electricity system.

The statement recalled that the planned restart of the G3 unit on 29 July had to be suspended after a technical fault was detected in a specialised seal on one of the steam turbine’s safety valves. The power plant emphasised that, thanks to the swift and well-coordinated efforts of its employees and technical partners, the unit was able to return to service safely in the shortest possible time.

World.title: Celebration: Hungary reopens railway line closed 3 years ago – videos, photos
World.content:
Passenger trains are once again running between Komló and Dombóvár, marking the reopening of another railway line closed under the previous government. Scheduled passenger services resumed on Saturday after a three-year suspension, with officials describing the occasion as a milestone for Hungarian rail transport.

The reopening was celebrated by thousands of local residents, train enthusiasts and passengers, who gathered in Komló as the historic Zobák Express, hauled by a legendary 424 steam locomotive, arrived at the station.

MÁV restores regular services

Speaking at the reopening ceremony, MÁV CEO Zsolt Hegyi said it was perhaps the first event he had attended where the celebration centred on the return of passenger trains to a railway line.

He confirmed that regular passenger services have officially resumed between Komló and Dombóvár and announced that rail services between Miskolc and Tiszaújváros will also return, with operations scheduled to restart on 1 September.

According to Hegyi, recent maintenance work restored the line for trains travelling at up to 60 km/h, eliminated speed restrictions and significantly improved the infrastructure. Over recent weeks, railway workers:

carried out track alignment works along more than 18 kilometres of railway,

repaired fastenings at over 6,500 concrete sleepers,

renovated the Komló railway station building, and

upgraded passenger information systems.

He added that further investment is planned, including modernising Komló station’s signalling equipment, which is expected to reduce the amount of time level crossings remain closed to road traffic.

Government promises end to railway closures

Transport and Construction Minister Dávid Vitézy, who travelled to Komló aboard the heritage train, thanked MÁV employees for completing the works in time for the reopening. He said the government had ended what he described as the previous era of railway closures and had entered a new period focused on railway development.

Calling rail transport the most sustainable and environmentally friendly mode of transport, Vitézy argued that train lines should be modernised rather than closed. He described the closure of the Komló line and nine other routes under the previous administration as a mistake, adding that more previously discontinued passenger services will be restored in the coming months.

The next reopening, he confirmed, will be the Miskolc–Tiszaújváros line from 1 September, while preparations are also underway to restore passenger traffic between Debrecen and Nagykereki.

If you missed it: Budapest landmarks to go dark: Parliament, Buda Castle and Citadella lights switched off

Thousands celebrate the return of trains

The reopening turned into a major public celebration, with hundreds of people lining the railway to welcome the steam train and several thousand gathering at Komló station. The Pécs Railway Concert Wind Orchestra performed during the festivities, while local residents, railway employees and members of parliament from Baranya and Tolna counties joined the celebrations.

In a later Facebook post, Vitézy said the enthusiastic turnout demonstrated that claims about a lack of demand for the railway had been proven wrong. “The people want to use the railway,” he wrote, adding that the government’s responsibility is now to provide reliable, high-quality rail services.

Local MP Áron Kovács described the reopening as more than just the return of a railway line, saying it was proof that the persistence of the local community had finally been rewarded.

World.title: Slovakian PM Fico offers to help Hungary with electricity as Paks shutdown threatens energy supply
World.content:
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has offered Slovakia’s support to Hungary as the country grapples with a deepening energy crisis caused by record-low water levels in the Danube that have severely reduced output at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

In a statement published on Facebook on Saturday, Fico said Slovakia was prepared to assist its southern neighbour should the situation at Paks worsen.

“I am closely monitoring the energy crisis in Hungary and would like to express our full solidarity with our neighbour and our readiness to help,” the Slovak prime minister wrote.

He warned that the possible shutdown of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant due to insufficient cooling water from the Danube could push Hungary into an “unprecedented energy crisis.”

Slovakia says its nuclear plants remain unaffected

Fico revealed that he had held consultations with Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Denisa Saková, as well as Branislav Strýček, CEO of Slovenské elektrárne, Slovakia’s state electricity producer.

According to the Slovak leader, the country’s two nuclear power stations — Mochovce and Jaslovské Bohunice — are operating normally and face no comparable risks because they use a different reactor cooling system.

Unlike Paks, which relies directly on water from the Danube to cool its reactors, Slovakia’s Mochovce nuclear plant uses cooling towers supplied by water from the Hron (Garam) River through a dedicated reservoir and dam system. This design makes it far less vulnerable to prolonged periods of low river levels and high summer temperatures.

If you missed it: Hungary prepares emergency power restrictions, Paks nuclear plant could shut down this weekend

Hungary continues emergency measures

Hungary has been implementing a series of emergency energy-saving measures after exceptionally low water levels forced repeated reductions in electricity generation at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

The government has already introduced restrictions affecting large industrial electricity consumers, reduced decorative lighting at public buildings, slowed metro and tram services in Budapest to save electricity, and announced temporary limits on rail freight operations during peak evening demand.

The restart of the Dunamenti Power Plant on Saturday restored nearly 400 MW of gas-fired generation capacity, providing an important boost to the national grid. However, the additional capacity does not fully compensate for the significant loss of nuclear generation at Paks, where output has fallen sharply because of the Danube’s historically low water level.

Fico’s offer highlights the close energy cooperation between the two neighbouring countries, whose electricity grids are interconnected as part of the Central European power network.

World.title: Premium property at Lake Balaton: what the numbers don’t tell you
World.content:
My previous columns covered the logic of Budapest’s premium market – from the step-by-step purchase process and discreet transactions to inheritance and the golden visa reality. This piece moves one step beyond the capital. Premium property at Lake Balaton has quietly overtaken Budapest in a telling metric: in 2024, the average sum spent per transaction on the northern shore reached HUF 67.7 million, against Budapest’s HUF 60.4 million average. The numbers, however, only show the surface. What lies behind them – the structure of supply, the legal constraints and the mechanism that has made this one of the most protected premium asset classes in Central Europe – is what genuinely deserves attention.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

Premium property at Lake Balaton: two very different markets

The Balaton property market divides sharply into two characters. The northern shore – Balatonfüred, the Tihany peninsula, Csopak, Badacsony, Balatonalmádi – is the prestige side: volcanic hills, a national park, historic wine regions and the inherited distinction of a 19th-century spa town. Average square-metre prices on the north shore moved between HUF 1.01 million and HUF 1.25 million in 2024; prime waterfront stock reached HUF 2–3.5 million per square metre. Tihany is in its own category: with an average of HUF 1.8–2.2 million per square metre it is one of the country’s most expensive settlements, and around 90 percent of its transactions close in cash.

The southern shore – Siófok, Zamárdi, Balatonszemes, Balatonlelle – has traditionally traded at lower prices. That hierarchy is shifting. In 2024, Balatonszemes reached HUF 1.55 million per square metre, making it the second most expensive Balaton settlement after Tihany; Szántód ranked third at HUF 1.53 million. The flatter southern topography allows direct-waterfront luxury villas and penthouse developments that are drawing increasing volumes of urban capital.

Balatonfüred: the capital of lakeside development

Balatonfüred has seen the most dramatic transformation of recent years. In the Fürdő utca district and the former Greek village area, luxury developments stand side by side, having added hundreds of premium homes to the market within a few years. Prices across the current new-build offering typically range from HUF 80 million at entry level to over HUF 400 million for top-floor and penthouse units, depending on location within the town, views and apartment size. These developments match international luxury standards in both scale and specification: underground parking, pools, saunas, smart-home systems and heat-pump engineering.

The Káli basin: where law creates value

Further inland from the lake, the Káli basin – Szentbékkálla, Köveskál, Monoszló, Kővágóörs – operates by a different logic entirely. A 2012-built luxury villa of 1,615 square metres on a ten-hectare vineyard estate with a wine cellar and pools in Monoszló is listed at close to HUF 2 billion, around €5 million. This is not exceptional; this is the area’s standard pricing logic.

The Káli Basin. Photo: premiumingatlanok.hu The Káli Basin. Photo: premiumingatlanok.hu

Behind these prices lies scarcity created not by the market but by regulation. The Káli basin falls within the Balaton Uplands National Park and the EU’s Natura 2000 network. Building coverage on rural plots is typically capped at three percent, and in many locations new building permits are simply not issued. The National Park was expanded by a further 8,500 hectares in April 2026. The supply of genuinely premium property at Lake Balaton and in the surrounding highlands is not growing – it is shrinking.

Tokaj-Hegyalja and Szekszárd: where wine country meets investment

Beyond the Balaton, Tokaj-Hegyalja is Hungary’s other rising premium market. Representative surveys consistently rank Tokaj as Hungarians’ favourite wine region, ahead of Eger and Villány. The area’s appeal rests on its natural landscape, the historic tradition of aszú production and a rapidly maturing premium gastronomy scene; long-established wineries and estate hotels have built an international-calibre tourism ecosystem that makes the region compelling even for the most discerning buyers. Average property prices here still trail the Balaton highlands, but sustained investment in infrastructure and gastronomic tourism is generating capital appreciation potential that few other Hungarian regions can match.

The wine-country premium market, however, does not end with Tokaj. Szekszárd – home of Bikavér and Kékfrankos, set in the historic heart of southern Transdanubia – is quietly moving onto the radar of considered buyers. The gently rolling loess hills, a near-Mediterranean microclimate and distinguished estates – among them Vesztergombi, Vida and Takler – offer a quality of life and sense of provenance that once seemed the exclusive preserve of the northern Balaton shore. What genuinely distinguishes the top tier of Szekszárd’s estate offering is sustainability as a real value dimension: at the finest properties, solar generation, heat-pump heating, a private well and a historic wine cellar are not separate features but components of a coherent, grid-independent ecosystem. At Szekszárd, a buyer is not yet paying Tihany prices, but a self-sustaining vineyard estate or country manor already represents an asset class whose supply cannot expand freely, constrained as it is by landscape and heritage protection.

Who is buying and why

According to KSH and ingatlan.com data, approximately 8,000 foreign nationals buy property in Hungary each year, with two-thirds of transactions now taking place outside Budapest. Among foreign buyers, Germans are the most active: their numbers grew by more than two-thirds in recent years, and every second German buyer chose the Balaton region – Somogy or Zala county. Price advantage is increasingly secondary as a motivation; macro-political stability, public safety and climate resilience have become the primary decision factors.

Hungary’s tax environment is a genuine draw. France, Spain and Norway operate annual wealth taxes that steadily erode invested capital; Hungary has no general net-wealth tax. Property taxation is limited to the one-off transfer duty and a local building tax – a position that compares favourably with the Mediterranean alternatives many buyers also consider.

Photo: premiumingatlanok.hu

What buyers need to know before stepping in

Entering Hungary’s rural premium market is considerably more complex than buying a Budapest apartment. The Agricultural Land Act draws a sharp distinction: non-EU nationals may not acquire farmland at all; EU nationals without a registered farmer qualification may acquire a maximum of one hectare of arable land, rising to 300 hectares with the relevant agricultural certification. Act XLVIII of 2025 – the Local Identity Act – has empowered municipalities to enforce pre-emption rights, restrict permanent registration and levy a settlement contribution on newcomers; over 200 municipalities already exercise these powers, and the effect is increasingly felt around the lake. On the other side of the ledger, the heritage building corporate tax incentive – which allows the cost of renovation to reduce the corporate tax base by twice the expenditure, producing a threefold tax-base reduction in practice – is one of the most powerful optimisation tools in the Hungarian legal system.

Position, not speculation

Premium property at Lake Balaton and in the Hungarian countryside has undergone a structural shift: it is no longer a seasonal asset but a standalone investment class. Supply is kept tight by conservation and legal constraints; demand is sustained by both domestic and international capital; and value growth rests on genuine scarcity rather than speculation. Anyone making meaningful decisions in this market needs more than price data – navigating the legal and physical landscape calls for experienced local representation, and that is the only reliable compass in a market this complex.

Emese Széll, an expert in the Hungarian premium real estate market. www.premiumingatlanok.com

This article is intended for general market and economic information purposes.

World.title: Hungary to suspend freight trains during evening peak to save electricity amid energy crisis
World.content:
Hungary will temporarily halt most rail freight traffic during the evening peak from Monday as the government introduces further emergency energy-saving measures following the sharp reduction in output at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant. The move is expected to reduce electricity demand by up to 90 megawatt-hours per day.

Evening freight rail services to be suspended

Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced in a video message on Saturday that the government had ordered the suspension of rail freight services between 5:00 PM and 10:00 PM from Monday.

According to the prime minister, the measure is designed to lower electricity consumption on the railway network during the most critical hours of the day and free up additional capacity for the national power grid.

Essential freight services exempt

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy said the restriction would apply to most freight trains, with exemptions only for services considered essential to the national economy or critical infrastructure. These include trains transporting supplies needed to keep power stations and other key facilities operating.

Vitézy noted that similar restrictions have previously been introduced during periods of heavy snowfall, when freight traffic was temporarily limited to help maintain railway operations.

Up to 90 MWh of electricity could be saved daily

Government estimates suggest the temporary suspension of freight traffic could save between 70 and 90 megawatt-hours (MWh) of electricity each day.

The measure forms part of a broader package of emergency actions introduced as Hungary prepares for a significant reduction in domestic electricity generation linked to the ongoing problems at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, whose output has been severely reduced due to the exceptionally low water level of the Danube.

Government expands energy-saving measures

Alongside the freight restrictions, the government has also announced:

Mandatory home working for eligible public administration employees during the first three days of next week.

A request for private-sector employers to allow remote working wherever possible and minimise office energy consumption.

The switch-off of decorative and non-essential lighting at all state institutions.

A call for all municipalities to implement the highest possible level of energy-saving measures.

Public urged to reduce electricity use

Vitézy also called on both businesses and households to cut electricity consumption wherever possible, particularly during the late afternoon and evening peak.

“Hungary is facing an unprecedented situation because of the shutdown of Paks, but with attention, cooperation and responsible decisions, we can keep the country running,” the minister said, urging the public to contribute to the nationwide effort.

The latest measures are part of the government’s wider response to an energy crisis triggered by the Danube’s historically low water levels, which have forced the gradual reduction of electricity generation at Hungary’s largest power plant.

World.title: Hungary recalls 25 more ambassadors, including from Washington, London, Brussels, Moscow and Kyiv
World.content:
Hungary has recalled another 25 ambassadors in one of the country’s biggest diplomatic reshuffles in recent years. The latest changes, initiated by Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, affect several of Hungary’s most strategically important diplomatic posts, including Washington, London, Brussels, Moscow and Kyiv.

Key diplomatic posts to change hands

The list of ambassadors whose appointments have been terminated was published in the latest issue of the Hungarian Gazette on Friday evening. Among the most high-profile recalls are Hungary’s ambassadors to:

Washington – Szabolcs Ferenc Takács

– Szabolcs Ferenc Takács London – Ferenc Kumin

– Ferenc Kumin Brussels – Tamás Iván Kovács

– Tamás Iván Kovács Moscow – Norbert Attila Konkoly

– Norbert Attila Konkoly Kyiv – Antal Heizer

– Antal Heizer Belgrade – József Zoltán Magyar

– József Zoltán Magyar Bratislava – Csaba Sándor Balogh

The changes also extend to Hungary’s permanent missions to major international organisations, including NATO, the United Nations, the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE).

Part of a broader diplomatic overhaul

This is the second major wave of ambassadorial recalls since the new government took office. At the end of June, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs ended the mandates of 37 heads of diplomatic missions, describing the changes as part of a wider professional renewal of Hungary’s diplomatic service.

At the time, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said the ministry aimed to build “a professional diplomatic corps operating at the highest standards” with ambassadors capable of advancing Hungary’s foreign policy objectives and strengthening the country’s international influence.

If you missed it: Hungarian FM Anita Orbán recalls dozens of ambassadors

Full list of recalled ambassadors

The latest round of recalls includes Hungary’s ambassadors or heads of mission in:

Brussels

Algiers

Belgrade

Doha

Moscow

Prague

Wellington

NATO (Brussels)

OSCE/UN (Vienna)

Bogotá

Baghdad

UN/WTO (Geneva)

The Hague

Yerevan

Kyiv

Copenhagen

London

Manila

Oslo

Bratislava

Pretoria

Sarajevo

Singapore

Tbilisi

Washington

Successors yet to be announced

The government has not yet named replacements for the outgoing ambassadors. The new nominees are expected to be announced after they complete the required parliamentary committee hearings, with further details on the transition process likely in the coming weeks.

World.title: Hungary regains nearly 400 MW as Dunamenti Power Plant returns to full capacity ahead of schedule!
World.content:
Hungary’s electricity system received a significant boost on Saturday after the Dunamenti Power Plant in Százhalombatta successfully returned to full operation following several days of repairs, restoring almost 400 megawatts of generating capacity during the country’s ongoing energy emergency.

The operator announced that the G3 generating unit resumed full-capacity operation on 1 August after successfully completing technical inspections and trial runs. The block was reconnected to the national electricity grid at 4:45 PM, making its nearly 400 MW of generation capacity available once again.

Earlier-than-expected restart

Prime Minister Péter Magyar welcomed the development in a Facebook post, describing it as “important news”.

“The Dunamenti Power Plant in Százhalombatta is back in operation after just three days thanks to rapid repair work. This provides an additional 360 MW of capacity. Thank you to everyone involved in the repairs,” the prime minister wrote.

Just a day earlier, Magyar had indicated that the plant was expected to resume operations on Sunday, meaning the restart came ahead of schedule.

Repairs delayed by technical fault

The G3 unit had originally been scheduled to restart on 29 July, but the process had to be suspended after engineers detected a technical fault in a specialised seal on one of the steam turbine’s protective valves. According to the operator, the unit could only be reconnected after the necessary repairs, extensive technical inspections and a successful trial operation had been completed.

Important support during the energy crisis

The restart comes as Hungary continues to face severe pressure on its electricity system due to exceptionally low water levels on the Danube, which have forced the gradual reduction of output at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

Although the restored capacity of the Dunamenti Power Plant significantly strengthens the national grid, it does not fully offset the latest loss at Paks. On Saturday alone, another turbine at the nuclear plant was taken offline because of the low river level, reducing Paks’ output by around 480 MW.

The Dunamenti Power Plant, owned by the MET Group since 2022, is Hungary’s largest gas-fired power station and has become a key element of the government’s efforts to maintain electricity supply during the current energy emergency.

World.title: Nscale to acquire Romanian co-founded AI startup Anyscale in reportedly USD 1.65 billion deal
World.content:
Cloud infrastructure provider Nscale will acquire AI software startup Anyscale, which has Romanian-born university professor Ion Stoica among its co-founders, in a transaction worth roughly USD 1.65 billion, according to a Bloomberg News source.

Ion Stoica is a co-founder of Anyscale, together with Robert Nishihara (chief executive officer) and Philipp Moritz (chief technology officer), who were his PhD students at RISELab within the University of California, Berkeley.

San Francisco-based Anyscale provides software for organizing and managing complex AI workloads so that they can run smoothly across multiple computers simultaneously. Nscale said it expects to attract more customers by offering Anyscale’s software.

Anyscale will continue to operate under its own brand and serve its existing customers, the companies said. Anyscale’s entire team of approximately 200 people across the United States, Europe and India will join Nscale as part of the acquisition.

The transaction is expected to be completed in the second half of this year, the companies said.

Anyscale recorded revenue growth of 70% compared with the previous quarter in the company’s most recent quarter, according to a blog post by its co-founders.

Originally from Romania, Stoica left for the United States in the late 1990s to pursue his PhD at Carnegie Mellon University. Since 2000, he has been teaching at UC Berkeley, where he leads a laboratory funded largely by technology companies such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google, and IBM, with an annual budget of more than USD 6 million.

Stoica became a billionaire by launching four startups that originated from his research laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley. The most valuable of them, Databricks and Anyscale, started as open-source projects within the university. The first was valued at USD 134 billion earlier this year.

Before Databricks, Stoica also co-founded video streaming startup Conviva.

World.title: UNICEF, Romanian Labor Ministry launch e-Learning HUB for professionals in social assistance
World.content:
Romania’s Labor Ministry and UNICEF announced the launch of e-Learning HUB, a national platform dedicated to the continuous professional training of personnel in the field of social services and sectors that contribute to social inclusion.

The HUB provides coordinated access to training opportunities, educational resources and professional development programs. The platform brings together continuous professional training opportunities for specialists in the social field, covering essential topics such as the protection of vulnerable persons, human rights, digital skills and quality standards in social services.

The HUB is designed to become the digital foundation of the future National Center for Continuous Training in Social Assistance, which is scheduled to become operational in 2028. The platform will contribute to increasing the skills of professionals in social assistance and related fields, personnel of central and local public authorities with responsibilities in the social field, decision-makers, accredited professional training providers, professional organizations, and non-governmental organizations active in the field of social assistance and the protection of human rights.

“Through e-Learning HUB, specialists across the country will be able to identify relevant courses more easily, develop their skills and have access to modern resources adapted to the real needs of the system,” said Silvia Dinică, State Secretary within the Labor Ministry.

“Professionals in social services are facing increasingly complex challenges, from poverty and social exclusion to the effects of recent crises on children and families. The e-Learning HUB platform offers a single access point to quality learning opportunities and represents an important step toward strengthening the workforce in the social field,” said Anna Riatti, UNICEF Representative in Romania.

The e-Learning HUB will facilitate access to accredited training programs, promote collaboration between institutions and training providers, and support the development of the skills needed to provide integrated and quality services.
